Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna said: Joseph stole a hen from among the birds that were in Jacob's house and gave it to a beggar.

Ka'b said: Joseph was alone in the house, and a beggar came to him, and in the house there was an ʿatāq (a female young goat), and he gave it to the beggar without his father's order. Wahb said: he used to set aside food from the table for the poor.

Hisham narrated from Sa'd ibn Zayd ibn Aslam concerning this verse: Joseph (peace be upon him) was with his mother at the house of a maternal uncle of his. He entered while he was a child playing, and took a small golden statue. That is the reproach of his brothers to him.

Ibn Ishaq narrated from Mujahid, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, who said: the first trial that befell Joseph, as it has reached me, was that his paternal aunt, the daughter of Isaac, who was the eldest of Isaac's children, had Isaac's girdle (mintaqa). They used to inherit it by seniority from their in-laws, and whoever held it had a sort of sovereignty that could not be contested, so he could do with it as he wished. Rachel, Joseph's mother, had died, so his aunt raised him and loved him intensely, and could not bear to be parted from him.

When he grew up and reached years of age, Jacob's love for him became strong. Jacob came to her and said: "O sister, hand Joseph over to me, for by Allah I cannot bear for him to be absent from me for an hour." She said: "No." He said: "By Allah, I will not leave him." She said: "Leave him with me for some days, that I may look at him, perhaps that will console me for him." He did so. When Jacob had left her, she took Isaac's girdle and tied it around Joseph beneath his clothes while he was young. Then she said: "The girdle of Isaac has been lost. Search for whoever took it." They searched but it was not found. She said: "Examine the people of the house." They examined them, and it was found with Joseph. She said: "By Allah, he is my bondsman; I may do with him as I wish." Jacob came to her and she told him the news. He said: "If he did that, then he is your bondsman. I can do nothing else." So she kept him, and Jacob could do nothing for him until she died. This is what Joseph's brothers meant when they said: ﴿If he steals, a brother of his has stolen before﴾, and this is the well-known proverb: "His excuse is worse than his crime."

﴿So Joseph kept it secret within himself﴾, he concealed it, ﴿and did not reveal it to them﴾. He used the feminine pronoun because he meant by it the word and the saying, and this is a recitation.

He said: ﴿You are worse in position﴾, i.e., worse in standing with Allah, than those whom you accuse of theft, in your conduct toward Joseph. ﴿And Allah knows best what you describe﴾, you say. Qatada said: "what you lie about."

The narrators said: When they entered upon Joseph, and the goblet was extracted from Benjamin's saddlebag, Joseph called for the goblet, struck it, and brought it close to his ear, then said: "Indeed, this goblet of mine informs me that you were twelve men, and that you set out with a brother of yours and sold him." When Benjamin heard this, he stood up and prostrated to Joseph, then said: "O King, ask your goblet of this brother of mine, where he is." He struck it and said: "Is he alive? You will see him." Benjamin said: "Do with me as you wish, for if he knows about me, he will rescue me." Joseph entered and wept, then performed ablution and came out. Benjamin said: "O King, I think you should strike your goblet, and it will tell you the truth about who stole it and placed it in my saddlebag." He struck it and said: "Indeed, this goblet of mine has disobeyed me, and it says: 'How do you ask me about my companion, when you have seen with whom you were?'"

He said: When the sons of Jacob grew angry, they could not be restrained. Rubayl grew angry and said: "By Allah, O King, either you release us, or I will cry out a cry that will leave no pregnant woman in Egypt without miscarrying what is in her womb." Every hair on Rubayl's body stood up, and he trembled from [......] [[unreadable word.]] Joseph touched him and his anger subsided. Rubayl said: "Who is this? In this land there is surely a seed from the seed of Jacob."

Joseph said: "And who is Jacob?" Rubayl became angry and said: "O King, do not mention Jacob, for he is the chosen one (sirr) of Allah, son of the sacrificed one (dhabīḥ) of Allah, son of the intimate friend (khalīl) of the Most Merciful." Joseph said: [Bear witness] if you are truthful.

Joseph held his brother, and by the judgment of his brothers he had more right to him than they did. They saw that there was no way to free him except by asking him to release him in exchange for something they would give him. ﴿They said: O Chief, indeed he has an aged father, [who is attached to his love]﴾, meaning Jacob. ﴿So take one of us in his place﴾, as a substitute. ﴿Indeed, we see you as one of the good-doers﴾ in your conduct. It was said: toward us. Ibn Ishaq said: they meant that if you do that, you will be among the good-doers.

He said: ﴿Allah forbid﴾, I seek refuge in Allah. It is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), and so the Arabs do with every verbal noun that stands in place of the verb. They say: "ḥamdan lillāh" (praise to Allah) and "shukran lillāh" (thanks to Allah), meaning "aḥmad Allāh" and "ashkuruh." ﴿That we should take only him with whom we found our property﴾, and he did not say "the one who stole," out of caution against lying. ﴿Indeed, then we would be wrongdoers﴾, if we took an innocent person for a guilty one.

﴿So when they despaired of him﴾, meaning they despaired of Joseph that he would answer what they asked, ﴿they withdrew to confer privately (najiyyan)﴾, i.e., they were alone with one another, consulting and conferring, with no others mixing with them. Najī is used for a group that confers, and it may also apply to one person. Allah said of one person: ﴿and We brought him near as a confidant (najiyyan)﴾ [Qur'an 19:52], and of the plural: ﴿they withdrew to confer privately (najiyyan)﴾. It is permissible for both the singular and the plural because it is a verbal noun used as an adjective, like "ʿadl" (justice), "zūr" (falsehood), "fiṭr" and the like. It derives from the saying: "najawtu fulānan anjūhu najiyyan" (I conferred with so-and-so privately). Similarly "najwā" is both a noun and a verbal noun. Allah said: ﴿and when they were in confidential talk (najwā)﴾ [Qur'an 17:47], i.e., conferring. He said: ﴿There is no private conference (najwā) of three﴾ [Qur'an 58:7], and of the verbal noun: ﴿Private conference is only from Satan﴾ [Qur'an 58:10]. A poet said:

"Banī Badā, the secret talk of men (khabb najwā al-rijāl),
(and) in your confidence be like the confidant's secret talk (khabb al-najiyy)."

In this verse, najwā and najiyy mean "consultation." The plural of najiyy is anjiya. Labid said:

"I witnessed the confidants of the stance (anjiyyat al-ifāqa), exalted,
My heels and the buttocks of the kings were witnesses."

Another said:

"Indeed, when the people are confidants (anjiya),
and their necks are shaking like ropes of a well-bucket,
there, advise me, and do not advise anyone else about him."

﴿The eldest of them said﴾, meaning in intellect and knowledge, not in age. He was Simeon (Shim'ūn), and he was their leader. This was said by Mujahid. Qatada, al-Suddi, al-Dahhak and Ka'b said: he was Rubayl, who was the oldest of them, and he was the cousin (son of the maternal aunt) of Joseph, and he was the one who forbade his brothers from killing him. Wahb and al-Kalbi said: Judah (Yahudha), who was the most intelligent of them. Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: Levi (Lāwī).

﴿Did you not know that your father took from you a solemn pledge (mawthiq) from Allah﴾, a covenant from Allah. ﴿And before this you neglected Joseph﴾. Scholars differed about the grammatical position of "mā" (what). Some said: it is in the accusative, governed by the verb of knowing, meaning: "Did you not know that before this, you neglected Joseph?" Others said: it is in the nominative, as the subject of a sentence, and the sentence is complete at His saying: ﴿from Allah﴾, meaning: "And before this, this is your neglect of Joseph," so "mā" is the subject, and its predicate is "wa-min qabl" (and before). It was also said: "mā" is a connecting particle (ṣila), and the meaning is "and from this, you neglected Joseph," i.e., you fell short and wasted him. It was also said: it is in the nominative as a predicate of a complete sentence.

﴿So I will not leave the land (arḍ) in which I am﴾, which is the land of Egypt, ﴿until my father permits me to leave it, or Allah judges for me﴾ to leave it, and leave my brother Benjamin there or with him; otherwise I will not leave it. Abu Salih said: "or Allah judges for me" with the sword, so that I may fight whoever has imprisoned my brother Benjamin.

﴿And He is the best of judges﴾, the most excellent and most just of those who decide between people.

The other brother, the one detained in Egypt, says this to his brothers: "Return to your father and say: 'O our father, your son Benjamin has stolen the goblet.'" Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak read *suriqa* (سُرِّق) with a ḍammah on the sīn, a kasrah on the rā' and a shaddah, in the passive form without a named agent (*mā lam yusamma fā'iluhu*). The meaning is that he was attributed to theft, like *khawwantuhu* (I accused him of betrayal) and *fajjartuhu* (I attributed immorality to him). That is, he was ascribed these qualities. [....]

"We bear witness only to what we know": this means that we never gave testimony at any time in our lives except to what we knew. This is not a testimony from us; rather, it is a report of the conduct of your son according to their claim. Ibn Ishaq said: its meaning is, "We only said that he stole because of what we knew." He said: the judgment among the prophets, Ya'qub and his sons, was that a thief should be enslaved for his theft.

"And we were not guardians of the unseen": Mujahid and Qatadah said: we did not know that your son would steal and that our affair would come to this. Had we known that, we would not have taken him with us. We only said, "We will guard our brother against what we have no means of guarding him against." Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, said: they meant that he stole at night while they were asleep, and that *al-ghayb* (the unseen) means the night in the language of Himyar. Ibn 'Abbas said: we did not know what he did by night or by day, or his coming and going. 'Ikrimah said: "And we were not guardians of the unseen" means: perhaps it was planted in his baggage at night.

It was also said that its meaning is: the theft was taken from his baggage while we were watching him, and we have no knowledge of the unseen; so perhaps they stole it and he did not steal. This is the meaning of the saying of Abu Ishaq. Ibn Kaysan said: we did not know that you would be afflicted as you were afflicted with Yusuf, and had we known that, we would not have taken your son and would not have gone away with him.

"And ask the town in which we were": that is, the people of the town, which is Egypt. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is a town among the towns of Egypt.

"And the caravan in which we came": that is, the caravan in which we were. There were with them people from Canaan, neighbours of Ya'qub (peace be upon him). Ibn Ishaq said: the brother detained in Egypt knew that his brothers were suspected by their father because of what they had done concerning his affair, so he instructed them to say this statement. "And indeed we are truthful."

He said: "Rather, your souls have made a matter attractive to you" — the verse is abridged in meaning. They returned to their father and told him that. He said: "Rather, your souls have made attractive to you a matter you desired." "So patience is beautiful. It may be that Allah will bring them all to me": Yusuf, Benjamin and their brother who remains in Egypt. "Indeed He is the All-Knowing of my grief and my longing over their loss, the All-Wise in the management of His creation."

They said: ﴿We miss the goblet of the king﴾. The reciters differed over how this is recited. Qathm narrated from Dawud ibn Abi Hind, from a client of the Banu Hashim, from Abu Hurayra that he recited ṣā' al-malik (صاع الملك). Abu Raja' recited ṣawʿ (صوع), and Yahya ibn Ma'mar recited ṣawgh (صوغ) with a ghayn. [It is said that] it is derived from ṣāgha, yaṣūghu, ṣawgh, and the plural of ṣawā' (صواع) is ṣiyaʿ, while the plural of ṣāʿ is aṣwāʿ.

﴿And for him who brings it, a camel's load [of grain]﴾, ﴿and I am its guarantor (zaʿīm)﴾. Zaʿīm means a guarantor, as the caller (mu'adhdhin) says. The root sense of zaʿīm is one who takes charge of a people's affairs, and a leader is also called zaʿīm. One says zaʿama, zaʿāma, and ziʿāman. Layla al-Akhyaliyya said:

"Until, when the banner was raised, I saw him
Beneath the banner, over the army, as a leader (zaʿīm)."

[Kitab al-'Ayn: 1/364.]

﴿They said﴾, meaning the brothers of Joseph: ﴿By Allah (tallāhi)﴾, i.e., ﴿wallāhi﴾. Its original is the letter waw, which was changed into tā', as the reciters did in taqwā, tukalān, turāb and tukhma. Its original is waw, and the waw in all these words is part of the noun, but in tallāhi it is not so, since it is only the waw of oath. The [Arab] usage became common on their tongues, and they considered the waw to be part of the letter itself, so they changed it into tā'. It was placed in this one word only, not in the other names of Allah, exalted is He.

﴿Indeed you know that we came not to cause corruption in the land, and we were not thieves﴾. If it is asked: from where did they know this?

The answer: al-Kalbi said that Joseph's servant, who was the caller (mu'adhdhin), said to them: "The king entrusted me with the goblet, and I fear the king's punishment. Today I have a good word to say to him. If I do not find it, I fear that my standing will fall and I will be disgraced in Egypt." They said: ﴿Indeed you know that we came not to cause corruption in the land﴾. Since we set out on this road we have not stayed with anyone, nor have we corrupted anything. Ask about us those whom we passed by: did we harm anyone, or did we spoil anything? We have also returned the money that we found in our saddlebags. If we were thieves, we would not have returned it.

Joseph's servant said: "It is the great goblet of the king, with which he measures." Some of them said: they only said that because they were known not to take what was not theirs. It was also said: when they entered Egypt they covered the mouths of their animals so that they would not eat from people's fields.

If it is asked: how did Joseph permit calling them thieves? It is answered that there are two answers. One is that he concealed in himself that they had stolen him from his father. The other is that it was the speech of the caller, not an order from Joseph, and Allah knows best.

﴿They said﴾, meaning the caller and his companions: ﴿What then shall be its penalty﴾, i.e., its recompense. Al-Akhfash said: if you wish, you may return the pronoun to the thieves, and if you wish, to the theft ﴿if you are liars﴾ in your saying: ﴿we were not thieves﴾.

They said: ﴿Its penalty is that he in whose saddlebag it is found, he himself shall be its penalty﴾, that the stolen property be handed over to the one from whom it was stolen, and he shall be enslaved for a year. This was the custom of the family of Jacob concerning the judgment for a thief. ﴿Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers﴾, those who do what is not theirs to do, by taking another's property through theft.

As for the grammatical construction, al-Farra' said: "man" (he who) is in the sense of "jazā'uhu" (its penalty). The meaning of man is raised by the pronoun that comes after it, and the answer of the conditional is the fa' in His saying ﴿fa-huwa jazā'uhu﴾ (then he himself is its penalty). The second "jazā'uhu" is raised by the implied meaning of the conditional and its answer. A similar usage in speech is when someone says: "What is due to me from you?" and the other replies: "For you from me is that, if you give me good news, you will have a thousand dirhams." It is as if he said: "For you from me is this." If you wish, the penalty may be raised by "man" alone and its relative clause, as if you said: "Its penalty is the one found in his saddlebag," as if you said: "Its recompense is that he be enslaved [in the future] also," so he said: ﴿fa-huwa jazā'uhu﴾. The summary of these sayings is: its penalty is the penalty of the one found in his saddlebag, or its penalty is the one found in his saddlebag. The sentence is complete.

He began with ﴿fa-huwa jazā'uhu﴾ and then the messenger said: "It is necessary to search your goods; you are not thieves until I search them." He then took them back to Joseph, and ﴿he began with their bags﴾ to remove suspicion, ﴿before the bag of his brother﴾. He had searched their goods one by one. Qatada said: we are told that he would not open any goods or look into any bag without seeking Allah's forgiveness, out of guilt for the accusation he had made against them. Until only the youth remained, he said: "I do not think this one took anything." His brothers said: "By Allah, we will not move until you search his saddlebag, for it is more pleasing to you and to us." When they opened his goods, they extracted it from them. That is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He took it out from his brother's bag﴾. The pronoun in His saying "istakhrajahā" (he extracted it) is feminine, while ṣuwā' (goblet) is masculine. Allah said: ﴿and for him who brings it, a camel's load﴾, because returning it to the water-vessel (al-siqāya) is like His saying: ﴿those who inherit the Firdaws﴾, then He said: ﴿therein they will abide forever﴾ [Qur'an 23:11], returning the pronoun to Paradise. And His saying:

"When the division is attended by the relatives, the orphans, and the needy,"
then He said: ﴿provide for them from it﴾ [Qur'an 4:8], i.e., from the inheritance.

It was also said: the pronoun returns to the theft. It was also said: He made it feminine because ṣuwā' is used as both masculine and feminine. Whoever made it feminine said: "thalāth aṣwuʿ" (three ṣāʿs) like "adūd" (cups), and whoever made it masculine said: "thalātha aṣwāʿ" (three ṣuwā's), like "thalātha athwāb" (three garments).

﴿Thus We devised for Joseph﴾, i.e., just as they acted at the beginning toward Joseph, We acted toward them. Allah related that Jacob said to Joseph: ﴿lest they plot against you a plot﴾ [Qur'an 12:5]. So the plot is the recompense of a plot. Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿thus We devised﴾ means "We did," al-Rabi' said: "We inspired," and Ibn al-Anbari said: "We willed."

The meaning of the verse: thus We acted for Joseph, until he took his brother to himself and separated him from his brothers by a pretext which Allah devised for him, and Joseph used it as a pretext. ﴿He could not have taken his brother in the king's religion﴾, i.e., in the king's judgment and ruling. This was said by Qatada. Ibn 'Abbas said: "in the king's authority." The root of dīn (religion) is obedience. The king's ruling concerning a thief was that he be enslaved, and that he pay double the value of what he stole to the one from whom it was stolen. Al-Dahhak said: when a thief was brought to the king, he would expose his buttocks and blind his eyes. ﴿Unless Allah wills﴾, i.e., Joseph would not have been able to take his brother Benjamin from among his brothers and hold him with him under the king's judgment, had it not been for what We devised for him through Our kindness, until he found the way to that, which was what he caused to be spoken on the tongues of his brothers, that the penalty for a thief is enslavement. So they acknowledged it and showed their willingness to hand over the brother to him. That was the intent of Joseph (peace be upon him). [See Fath al-Qadir: 3/43.]

﴿We raise by degrees whom We will﴾, by knowledge, just as We raised Joseph above his brothers.

﴿And above every possessor of knowledge is one who knows﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: this one is more knowing than that one, and that one is more knowing than this one, and Allah is above every knower. Qatada and al-Hasan said: by Allah, there is no scholar on the face of the earth but that above him is one more knowing than he, until knowledge reaches Allah, who taught it, and from Him it began and to Him it returns. In the recitation of 'Abd Allah it is: "wa fawqa kulli dhī ʿilmin ʿalīm" (and above every knower is one who knows).

It is narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi that 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah honor his face, gave a judgment in a case, and a man from the side of the mosque said: "O Commander of the Faithful, the judgment is not as you have judged." He said: "Then what is it?" He said: "Such and such." He said: "You are right and you are wrong!!" ﴿And above every possessor of knowledge is one who knows﴾.

They said: When the goblet was taken out of Benjamin's saddlebag, his brothers lowered their heads out of shame and turned to Benjamin and said: "O Benjamin, what is this that you have done? You have disgraced us and blackened our faces. O sons of Rachel, you are never free of trouble from us. When did you take the goblet?"

Benjamin said: "Rather, the sons of Rachel are those from whom you are never free of trouble. You took my brother and destroyed him in the wilderness. This goblet was placed in my saddlebag by the one who placed the dirhams in your saddlebags."

Then they said to Joseph: ﴿If he steals, a brother of his has stolen before﴾, i.e., from his father and mother, before. Scholars differed about the theft with which they charged Joseph. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatada said: Joseph stole an idol belonging to his maternal grandfather, broke it, and threw it on the road. Al-Kalbi said: his mother sent him when she wanted to leave Haran with Jacob for Palestine and Jordan. She ordered him to go and take a jar in which there were idols belonging to her son, so that when his father missed them he would become Muslim. He went, took it, and brought it to his mother. This is the theft they mean.

It is narrated from Ibn Juraij: Joseph's mother ordered him to steal an idol belonging to his maternal uncle which he worshipped, and she was a Muslim. Abu Kurayb narrated from Abu Idris who said: I heard my father say: the children of Jacob were at a meal, and Joseph looked at a bone (ʿirq), and hid it, so they reproached him for that. 'Abd Allah ibn al-Sadi narrated, from his father, from Mujahid, that a beggar came to the house, and Joseph stole a [garment] from the house and gave it to the beggar, so they reproached him for it. Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna said: Joseph stole a hen from among the birds that were in Jacob's house and gave it to a beggar.

Ka'b said: Joseph was alone in the house, and a beggar came to him, and in the house there was an ʿatāq (a female young goat), and he gave it to the beggar without his father's order. Wahb said: he used to set aside food from the table for the poor.

Hisham narrated from Sa'd ibn Zayd ibn Aslam concerning this verse: Joseph (peace be upon him) was with his mother at the house of a maternal uncle of his. He entered while he was a child playing, and took a small golden statue. That is the reproach of his brothers to him.

Ibn Ishaq narrated from Mujahid, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, who said: the first trial that befell Joseph, as it has reached me, was that his paternal aunt, the daughter of Isaac, who was the eldest of Isaac's children, had Isaac's girdle (mintaqa). They used to inherit it by seniority from their in-laws, and whoever held it had a sort of sovereignty that could not be contested, so he could do with it as he wished. Rachel, Joseph's mother, had died, so his aunt raised him and loved him intensely, and could not bear to be parted from him.

When he grew up and reached years of age, Jacob's love for him became strong. Jacob came to her and said: "O sister, hand Joseph over to me, for by Allah I cannot bear for him to be absent from me for an hour." She said: "No." He said: "By Allah, I will not leave him." She said: "Leave him with me for some days, that I may look at him, perhaps that will console me for him." He did so. When Jacob had left her, she took Isaac's girdle and tied it around Joseph beneath his clothes while he was young. Then she said: "The girdle of Isaac has been lost. Search for whoever took it." They searched but it was not found. She said: "Examine the people of the house." They examined them, and it was found with Joseph. She said: "By Allah, he is my bondsman; I may do with him as I wish." Jacob came to her and she told him the news. He said: "If he did that, then he is your bondsman. I can do nothing else." So she kept him, and Jacob could do nothing for him until she died. This is what Joseph's brothers meant when they said: ﴿If he steals, a brother of his has stolen before﴾, and this is the well-known proverb: "His excuse is worse than his crime."

﴿So Joseph kept it secret within himself﴾, he concealed it, ﴿and did not reveal it to them﴾. He used the feminine pronoun because he meant by it the word and the saying, and this is a recitation.

He said: ﴿You are worse in position﴾, i.e., worse in standing with Allah, than those whom you accuse of theft, in your conduct toward Joseph. ﴿And Allah knows best what you describe﴾, you say. Qatada said: "what you lie about."

The narrators said: When they entered upon Joseph, and the goblet was extracted from Benjamin's saddlebag, Joseph called for the goblet, struck it, and brought it close to his ear, then said: "Indeed, this goblet of mine informs me that you were twelve men, and that you set out with a brother of yours and sold him." When Benjamin heard this, he stood up and prostrated to Joseph, then said: "O King, ask your goblet of this brother of mine, where he is." He struck it and said: "Is he alive? You will see him." Benjamin said: "Do with me as you wish, for if he knows about me, he will rescue me." Joseph entered and wept, then performed ablution and came out. Benjamin said: "O King, I think you should strike your goblet, and it will tell you the truth about who stole it and placed it in my saddlebag." He struck it and said: "Indeed, this goblet of mine has disobeyed me, and it says: 'How do you ask me about my companion, when you have seen with whom you were?'"

He said: When the sons of Jacob grew angry, they could not be restrained. Rubayl grew angry and said: "By Allah, O King, either you release us, or I will cry out a cry that will leave no pregnant woman in Egypt without miscarrying what is in her womb." Every hair on Rubayl's body stood up, and he trembled from [......] [[unreadable word.]] Joseph touched him and his anger subsided. Rubayl said: "Who is this? In this land there is surely a seed from the seed of Jacob."

Joseph said: "And who is Jacob?" Rubayl became angry and said: "O King, do not mention Jacob, for he is the chosen one (sirr) of Allah, son of the sacrificed one (dhabīḥ) of Allah, son of the intimate friend (khalīl) of the Most Merciful." Joseph said: [Bear witness] if you are truthful.

Joseph held his brother, and by the judgment of his brothers he had more right to him than they did. They saw that there was no way to free him except by asking him to release him in exchange for something they would give him. ﴿They said: O Chief, indeed he has an aged father, [who is attached to his love]﴾, meaning Jacob. ﴿So take one of us in his place﴾, as a substitute. ﴿Indeed, we see you as one of the good-doers﴾ in your conduct. It was said: toward us. Ibn Ishaq said: they meant that if you do that, you will be among the good-doers.

He said: ﴿Allah forbid﴾, I seek refuge in Allah. It is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), and so the Arabs do with every verbal noun that stands in place of the verb. They say: "ḥamdan lillāh" (praise to Allah) and "shukran lillāh" (thanks to Allah), meaning "aḥmad Allāh" and "ashkuruh." ﴿That we should take only him with whom we found our property﴾, and he did not say "the one who stole," out of caution against lying. ﴿Indeed, then we would be wrongdoers﴾, if we took an innocent person for a guilty one.

﴿So when they despaired of him﴾, meaning they despaired of Joseph that he would answer what they asked, ﴿they withdrew to confer privately (najiyyan)﴾, i.e., they were alone with one another, consulting and conferring, with no others mixing with them. Najī is used for a group that confers, and it may also apply to one person. Allah said of one person: ﴿and We brought him near as a confidant (najiyyan)﴾ [Qur'an 19:52], and of the plural: ﴿they withdrew to confer privately (najiyyan)﴾. It is permissible for both the singular and the plural because it is a verbal noun used as an adjective, like "ʿadl" (justice), "zūr" (falsehood), "fiṭr" and the like. It derives from the saying: "najawtu fulānan anjūhu najiyyan" (I conferred with so-and-so privately). Similarly "najwā" is both a noun and a verbal noun. Allah said: ﴿and when they were in confidential talk (najwā)﴾ [Qur'an 17:47], i.e., conferring. He said: ﴿There is no private conference (najwā) of three﴾ [Qur'an 58:7], and of the verbal noun: ﴿Private conference is only from Satan﴾ [Qur'an 58:10]. A poet said:

"Banī Badā, the secret talk of men (khabb najwā al-rijāl),
(and) in your confidence be like the confidant's secret talk (khabb al-najiyy)."

In this verse, najwā and najiyy mean "consultation." The plural of najiyy is anjiya. Labid said:

"I witnessed the confidants of the stance (anjiyyat al-ifāqa), exalted,
My heels and the buttocks of the kings were witnesses."

Another said:

"Indeed, when the people are confidants (anjiya),
and their necks are shaking like ropes of a well-bucket,
there, advise me, and do not advise anyone else about him."

﴿The eldest of them said﴾, meaning in intellect and knowledge, not in age. He was Simeon (Shim'ūn), and he was their leader. This was said by Mujahid. Qatada, al-Suddi, al-Dahhak and Ka'b said: he was Rubayl, who was the oldest of them, and he was the cousin (son of the maternal aunt) of Joseph, and he was the one who forbade his brothers from killing him. Wahb and al-Kalbi said: Judah (Yahudha), who was the most intelligent of them. Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: Levi (Lāwī).

﴿Did you not know that your father took from you a solemn pledge (mawthiq) from Allah﴾, a covenant from Allah. ﴿And before this you neglected Joseph﴾. Scholars differed about the grammatical position of "mā" (what). Some said: it is in the accusative, governed by the verb of knowing, meaning: "Did you not know that before this, you neglected Joseph?" Others said: it is in the nominative, as the subject of a sentence, and the sentence is complete at His saying: ﴿from Allah﴾, meaning: "And before this, this is your neglect of Joseph," so "mā" is the subject, and its predicate is "wa-min qabl" (and before). It was also said: "mā" is a connecting particle (ṣila), and the meaning is "and from this, you neglected Joseph," i.e., you fell short and wasted him. It was also said: it is in the nominative as a predicate of a complete sentence.

﴿So I will not leave the land (arḍ) in which I am﴾, which is the land of Egypt, ﴿until my father permits me to leave it, or Allah judges for me﴾ to leave it, and leave my brother Benjamin there or with him; otherwise I will not leave it. Abu Salih said: "or Allah judges for me" with the sword, so that I may fight whoever has imprisoned my brother Benjamin.

﴿And He is the best of judges﴾, the most excellent and most just of those who decide between people.

The other brother, the one detained in Egypt, says this to his brothers: "Return to your father and say: 'O our father, your son Benjamin has stolen the goblet.'" Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak read *suriqa* (سُرِّق) with a ḍammah on the sīn, a kasrah on the rā' and a shaddah, in the passive form without a named agent (*mā lam yusamma fā'iluhu*). The meaning is that he was attributed to theft, like *khawwantuhu* (I accused him of betrayal) and *fajjartuhu* (I attributed immorality to him). That is, he was ascribed these qualities. [....]

"We bear witness only to what we know": this means that we never gave testimony at any time in our lives except to what we knew. This is not a testimony from us; rather, it is a report of the conduct of your son according to their claim. Ibn Ishaq said: its meaning is, "We only said that he stole because of what we knew." He said: the judgment among the prophets, Ya'qub and his sons, was that a thief should be enslaved for his theft.

"And we were not guardians of the unseen": Mujahid and Qatadah said: we did not know that your son would steal and that our affair would come to this. Had we known that, we would not have taken him with us. We only said, "We will guard our brother against what we have no means of guarding him against." Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, said: they meant that he stole at night while they were asleep, and that *al-ghayb* (the unseen) means the night in the language of Himyar. Ibn 'Abbas said: we did not know what he did by night or by day, or his coming and going. 'Ikrimah said: "And we were not guardians of the unseen" means: perhaps it was planted in his baggage at night.

It was also said that its meaning is: the theft was taken from his baggage while we were watching him, and we have no knowledge of the unseen; so perhaps they stole it and he did not steal. This is the meaning of the saying of Abu Ishaq. Ibn Kaysan said: we did not know that you would be afflicted as you were afflicted with Yusuf, and had we known that, we would not have taken your son and would not have gone away with him.

"And ask the town in which we were": that is, the people of the town, which is Egypt. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is a town among the towns of Egypt.

"And the caravan in which we came": that is, the caravan in which we were. There were with them people from Canaan, neighbours of Ya'qub (peace be upon him). Ibn Ishaq said: the brother detained in Egypt knew that his brothers were suspected by their father because of what they had done concerning his affair, so he instructed them to say this statement. "And indeed we are truthful."

He said: "Rather, your souls have made a matter attractive to you" — the verse is abridged in meaning. They returned to their father and told him that. He said: "Rather, your souls have made attractive to you a matter you desired." "So patience is beautiful. It may be that Allah will bring them all to me": Yusuf, Benjamin and their brother who remains in Egypt. "Indeed He is the All-Knowing of my grief and my longing over their loss, the All-Wise in the management of His creation."

They said: ﴿We miss the goblet of the king﴾. The reciters differed over how this is recited. Qathm narrated from Dawud ibn Abi Hind, from a client of the Banu Hashim, from Abu Hurayra that he recited ṣā' al-malik (صاع الملك). Abu Raja' recited ṣawʿ (صوع), and Yahya ibn Ma'mar recited ṣawgh (صوغ) with a ghayn. [It is said that] it is derived from ṣāgha, yaṣūghu, ṣawgh, and the plural of ṣawā' (صواع) is ṣiyaʿ, while the plural of ṣāʿ is aṣwāʿ.

﴿And for him who brings it, a camel's load [of grain]﴾, ﴿and I am its guarantor (zaʿīm)﴾. Zaʿīm means a guarantor, as the caller (mu'adhdhin) says. The root sense of zaʿīm is one who takes charge of a people's affairs, and a leader is also called zaʿīm. One says zaʿama, zaʿāma, and ziʿāman. Layla al-Akhyaliyya said:

"Until, when the banner was raised, I saw him
Beneath the banner, over the army, as a leader (zaʿīm)."

[Kitab al-'Ayn: 1/364.]

﴿They said﴾, meaning the brothers of Joseph: ﴿By Allah (tallāhi)﴾, i.e., ﴿wallāhi﴾. Its original is the letter waw, which was changed into tā', as the reciters did in taqwā, tukalān, turāb and tukhma. Its original is waw, and the waw in all these words is part of the noun, but in tallāhi it is not so, since it is only the waw of oath. The [Arab] usage became common on their tongues, and they considered the waw to be part of the letter itself, so they changed it into tā'. It was placed in this one word only, not in the other names of Allah, exalted is He.

﴿Indeed you know that we came not to cause corruption in the land, and we were not thieves﴾. If it is asked: from where did they know this?

The answer: al-Kalbi said that Joseph's servant, who was the caller (mu'adhdhin), said to them: "The king entrusted me with the goblet, and I fear the king's punishment. Today I have a good word to say to him. If I do not find it, I fear that my standing will fall and I will be disgraced in Egypt." They said: ﴿Indeed you know that we came not to cause corruption in the land﴾. Since we set out on this road we have not stayed with anyone, nor have we corrupted anything. Ask about us those whom we passed by: did we harm anyone, or did we spoil anything? We have also returned the money that we found in our saddlebags. If we were thieves, we would not have returned it.

Joseph's servant said: "It is the great goblet of the king, with which he measures." Some of them said: they only said that because they were known not to take what was not theirs. It was also said: when they entered Egypt they covered the mouths of their animals so that they would not eat from people's fields.

If it is asked: how did Joseph permit calling them thieves? It is answered that there are two answers. One is that he concealed in himself that they had stolen him from his father. The other is that it was the speech of the caller, not an order from Joseph, and Allah knows best.

﴿They said﴾, meaning the caller and his companions: ﴿What then shall be its penalty﴾, i.e., its recompense. Al-Akhfash said: if you wish, you may return the pronoun to the thieves, and if you wish, to the theft ﴿if you are liars﴾ in your saying: ﴿we were not thieves﴾.

They said: ﴿Its penalty is that he in whose saddlebag it is found, he himself shall be its penalty﴾, that the stolen property be handed over to the one from whom it was stolen, and he shall be enslaved for a year. This was the custom of the family of Jacob concerning the judgment for a thief. ﴿Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers﴾, those who do what is not theirs to do, by taking another's property through theft.

As for the grammatical construction, al-Farra' said: "man" (he who) is in the sense of "jazā'uhu" (its penalty). The meaning of man is raised by the pronoun that comes after it, and the answer of the conditional is the fa' in His saying ﴿fa-huwa jazā'uhu﴾ (then he himself is its penalty). The second "jazā'uhu" is raised by the implied meaning of the conditional and its answer. A similar usage in speech is when someone says: "What is due to me from you?" and the other replies: "For you from me is that, if you give me good news, you will have a thousand dirhams." It is as if he said: "For you from me is this." If you wish, the penalty may be raised by "man" alone and its relative clause, as if you said: "Its penalty is the one found in his saddlebag," as if you said: "Its recompense is that he be enslaved [in the future] also," so he said: ﴿fa-huwa jazā'uhu﴾. The summary of these sayings is: its penalty is the penalty of the one found in his saddlebag, or its penalty is the one found in his saddlebag. The sentence is complete.

He began with ﴿fa-huwa jazā'uhu﴾ and then the messenger said: "It is necessary to search your goods; you are not thieves until I search them." He then took them back to Joseph, and ﴿he began with their bags﴾ to remove suspicion, ﴿before the bag of his brother﴾. He had searched their goods one by one. Qatada said: we are told that he would not open any goods or look into any bag without seeking Allah's forgiveness, out of guilt for the accusation he had made against them. Until only the youth remained, he said: "I do not think this one took anything." His brothers said: "By Allah, we will not move until you search his saddlebag, for it is more pleasing to you and to us." When they opened his goods, they extracted it from them. That is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He took it out from his brother's bag﴾. The pronoun in His saying "istakhrajahā" (he extracted it) is feminine, while ṣuwā' (goblet) is masculine. Allah said: ﴿and for him who brings it, a camel's load﴾, because returning it to the water-vessel (al-siqāya) is like His saying: ﴿those who inherit the Firdaws﴾, then He said: ﴿therein they will abide forever﴾ [Qur'an 23:11], returning the pronoun to Paradise. And His saying:

"When the division is attended by the relatives, the orphans, and the needy,"
then He said: ﴿provide for them from it﴾ [Qur'an 4:8], i.e., from the inheritance.

It was also said: the pronoun returns to the theft. It was also said: He made it feminine because ṣuwā' is used as both masculine and feminine. Whoever made it feminine said: "thalāth aṣwuʿ" (three ṣāʿs) like "adūd" (cups), and whoever made it masculine said: "thalātha aṣwāʿ" (three ṣuwā's), like "thalātha athwāb" (three garments).

﴿Thus We devised for Joseph﴾, i.e., just as they acted at the beginning toward Joseph, We acted toward them. Allah related that Jacob said to Joseph: ﴿lest they plot against you a plot﴾ [Qur'an 12:5]. So the plot is the recompense of a plot. Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿thus We devised﴾ means "We did," al-Rabi' said: "We inspired," and Ibn al-Anbari said: "We willed."

The meaning of the verse: thus We acted for Joseph, until he took his brother to himself and separated him from his brothers by a pretext which Allah devised for him, and Joseph used it as a pretext. ﴿He could not have taken his brother in the king's religion﴾, i.e., in the king's judgment and ruling. This was said by Qatada. Ibn 'Abbas said: "in the king's authority." The root of dīn (religion) is obedience. The king's ruling concerning a thief was that he be enslaved, and that he pay double the value of what he stole to the one from whom it was stolen. Al-Dahhak said: when a thief was brought to the king, he would expose his buttocks and blind his eyes. ﴿Unless Allah wills﴾, i.e., Joseph would not have been able to take his brother Benjamin from among his brothers and hold him with him under the king's judgment, had it not been for what We devised for him through Our kindness, until he found the way to that, which was what he caused to be spoken on the tongues of his brothers, that the penalty for a thief is enslavement. So they acknowledged it and showed their willingness to hand over the brother to him. That was the intent of Joseph (peace be upon him). [See Fath al-Qadir: 3/43.]

﴿We raise by degrees whom We will﴾, by knowledge, just as We raised Joseph above his brothers.

﴿And above every possessor of knowledge is one who knows﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: this one is more knowing than that one, and that one is more knowing than this one, and Allah is above every knower. Qatada and al-Hasan said: by Allah, there is no scholar on the face of the earth but that above him is one more knowing than he, until knowledge reaches Allah, who taught it, and from Him it began and to Him it returns. In the recitation of 'Abd Allah it is: "wa fawqa kulli dhī ʿilmin ʿalīm" (and above every knower is one who knows).

It is narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi that 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah honor his face, gave a judgment in a case, and a man from the side of the mosque said: "O Commander of the Faithful, the judgment is not as you have judged." He said: "Then what is it?" He said: "Such and such." He said: "You are right and you are wrong!!" ﴿And above every possessor of knowledge is one who knows﴾.

They said: When the goblet was taken out of Benjamin's saddlebag, his brothers lowered their heads out of shame and turned to Benjamin and said: "O Benjamin, what is this that you have done? You have disgraced us and blackened our faces. O sons of Rachel, you are never free of trouble from us. When did you take the goblet?"

Benjamin said: "Rather, the sons of Rachel are those from whom you are never free of trouble. You took my brother and destroyed him in the wilderness. This goblet was placed in my saddlebag by the one who placed the dirhams in your saddlebags."

Then they said to Joseph: ﴿If he steals, a brother of his has stolen before﴾, i.e., from his father and mother, before. Scholars differed about the theft with which they charged Joseph. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatada said: Joseph stole an idol belonging to his maternal grandfather, broke it, and threw it on the road. Al-Kalbi said: his mother sent him when she wanted to leave Haran with Jacob for Palestine and Jordan. She ordered him to go and take a jar in which there were idols belonging to her son, so that when his father missed them he would become Muslim. He went, took it, and brought it to his mother. This is the theft they mean.

It is narrated from Ibn Juraij: Joseph's mother ordered him to steal an idol belonging to his maternal uncle which he worshipped, and she was a Muslim. Abu Kurayb narrated from Abu Idris who said: I heard my father say: the children of Jacob were at a meal, and Joseph looked at a bone (ʿirq), and hid it, so they reproached him for that. 'Abd Allah ibn al-Sadi narrated, from his father, from Mujahid, that a beggar came to the house, and Joseph stole a [garment] from the house and gave it to the beggar, so they reproached him for it. Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna said: Joseph stole a hen from among the birds that were in Jacob's house and gave it to a beggar.

Ka'b said: Joseph was alone in the house, and a beggar came to him, and in the house there was an ʿatāq (a female young goat), and he gave it to the beggar without his father's order. Wahb said: he used to set aside food from the table for the poor.

Hisham narrated from Sa'd ibn Zayd ibn Aslam concerning this verse: Joseph (peace be upon him) was with his mother at the house of a maternal uncle of his. He entered while he was a child playing, and took a small golden statue. That is the reproach of his brothers to him.

Ibn Ishaq narrated from Mujahid, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, who said: the first trial that befell Joseph, as it has reached me, was that his paternal aunt, the daughter of Isaac, who was the eldest of Isaac's children, had Isaac's girdle (mintaqa). They used to inherit it by seniority from their in-laws, and whoever held it had a sort of sovereignty that could not be contested, so he could do with it as he wished. Rachel, Joseph's mother, had died, so his aunt raised him and loved him intensely, and could not bear to be parted from him.

When he grew up and reached years of age, Jacob's love for him became strong. Jacob came to her and said: "O sister, hand Joseph over to me, for by Allah I cannot bear for him to be absent from me for an hour." She said: "No." He said: "By Allah, I will not leave him." She said: "Leave him with me for some days, that I may look at him, perhaps that will console me for him." He did so. When Jacob had left her, she took Isaac's girdle and tied it around Joseph beneath his clothes while he was young. Then she said: "The girdle of Isaac has been lost. Search for whoever took it." They searched but it was not found. She said: "Examine the people of the house." They examined them, and it was found with Joseph. She said: "By Allah, he is my bondsman; I may do with him as I wish." Jacob came to her and she told him the news. He said: "If he did that, then he is your bondsman. I can do nothing else." So she kept him, and Jacob could do nothing for him until she died. This is what Joseph's brothers meant when they said: ﴿If he steals, a brother of his has stolen before﴾, and this is the well-known proverb: "His excuse is worse than his crime."

﴿So Joseph kept it secret within himself﴾, he concealed it, ﴿and did not reveal it to them﴾. He used the feminine pronoun because he meant by it the word and the saying, and this is a recitation.

He said: ﴿You are worse in position﴾, i.e., worse in standing with Allah, than those whom you accuse of theft, in your conduct toward Joseph. ﴿And Allah knows best what you describe﴾, you say. Qatada said: "what you lie about."

The narrators said: When they entered upon Joseph, and the goblet was extracted from Benjamin's saddlebag, Joseph called for the goblet, struck it, and brought it close to his ear, then said: "Indeed, this goblet of mine informs me that you were twelve men, and that you set out with a brother of yours and sold him." When Benjamin heard this, he stood up and prostrated to Joseph, then said: "O King, ask your goblet of this brother of mine, where he is." He struck it and said: "Is he alive? You will see him." Benjamin said: "Do with me as you wish, for if he knows about me, he will rescue me." Joseph entered and wept, then performed ablution and came out. Benjamin said: "O King, I think you should strike your goblet, and it will tell you the truth about who stole it and placed it in my saddlebag." He struck it and said: "Indeed, this goblet of mine has disobeyed me, and it says: 'How do you ask me about my companion, when you have seen with whom you were?'"

He said: When the sons of Jacob grew angry, they could not be restrained. Rubayl grew angry and said: "By Allah, O King, either you release us, or I will cry out a cry that will leave no pregnant woman in Egypt without miscarrying what is in her womb." Every hair on Rubayl's body stood up, and he trembled from [......] [[unreadable word.]] Joseph touched him and his anger subsided. Rubayl said: "Who is this? In this land there is surely a seed from the seed of Jacob."

Joseph said: "And who is Jacob?" Rubayl became angry and said: "O King, do not mention Jacob, for he is the chosen one (sirr) of Allah, son of the sacrificed one (dhabīḥ) of Allah, son of the intimate friend (khalīl) of the Most Merciful." Joseph said: [Bear witness] if you are truthful.

Joseph held his brother, and by the judgment of his brothers he had more right to him than they did. They saw that there was no way to free him except by asking him to release him in exchange for something they would give him. ﴿They said: O Chief, indeed he has an aged father, [who is attached to his love]﴾, meaning Jacob. ﴿So take one of us in his place﴾, as a substitute. ﴿Indeed, we see you as one of the good-doers﴾ in your conduct. It was said: toward us. Ibn Ishaq said: they meant that if you do that, you will be among the good-doers.

He said: ﴿Allah forbid﴾, I seek refuge in Allah. It is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), and so the Arabs do with every verbal noun that stands in place of the verb. They say: "ḥamdan lillāh" (praise to Allah) and "shukran lillāh" (thanks to Allah), meaning "aḥmad Allāh" and "ashkuruh." ﴿That we should take only him with whom we found our property﴾, and he did not say "the one who stole," out of caution against lying. ﴿Indeed, then we would be wrongdoers﴾, if we took an innocent person for a guilty one.

﴿So when they despaired of him﴾, meaning they despaired of Joseph that he would answer what they asked, ﴿they withdrew to confer privately (najiyyan)﴾, i.e., they were alone with one another, consulting and conferring, with no others mixing with them. Najī is used for a group that confers, and it may also apply to one person. Allah said of one person: ﴿and We brought him near as a confidant (najiyyan)﴾ [Qur'an 19:52], and of the plural: ﴿they withdrew to confer privately (najiyyan)﴾. It is permissible for both the singular and the plural because it is a verbal noun used as an adjective, like "ʿadl" (justice), "zūr" (falsehood), "fiṭr" and the like. It derives from the saying: "najawtu fulānan anjūhu najiyyan" (I conferred with so-and-so privately). Similarly "najwā" is both a noun and a verbal noun. Allah said: ﴿and when they were in confidential talk (najwā)﴾ [Qur'an 17:47], i.e., conferring. He said: ﴿There is no private conference (najwā) of three﴾ [Qur'an 58:7], and of the verbal noun: ﴿Private conference is only from Satan﴾ [Qur'an 58:10]. A poet said:

"Banī Badā, the secret talk of men (khabb najwā al-rijāl),
(and) in your confidence be like the confidant's secret talk (khabb al-najiyy)."

In this verse, najwā and najiyy mean "consultation." The plural of najiyy is anjiya. Labid said:

"I witnessed the confidants of the stance (anjiyyat al-ifāqa), exalted,
My heels and the buttocks of the kings were witnesses."

Another said:

"Indeed, when the people are confidants (anjiya),
and their necks are shaking like ropes of a well-bucket,
there, advise me, and do not advise anyone else about him."

﴿The eldest of them said﴾, meaning in intellect and knowledge, not in age. He was Simeon (Shim'ūn), and he was their leader. This was said by Mujahid. Qatada, al-Suddi, al-Dahhak and Ka'b said: he was Rubayl, who was the oldest of them, and he was the cousin (son of the maternal aunt) of Joseph, and he was the one who forbade his brothers from killing him. Wahb and al-Kalbi said: Judah (Yahudha), who was the most intelligent of them. Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: Levi (Lāwī).

﴿Did you not know that your father took from you a solemn pledge (mawthiq) from Allah﴾, a covenant from Allah. ﴿And before this you neglected Joseph﴾. Scholars differed about the grammatical position of "mā" (what). Some said: it is in the accusative, governed by the verb of knowing, meaning: "Did you not know that before this, you neglected Joseph?" Others said: it is in the nominative, as the subject of a sentence, and the sentence is complete at His saying: ﴿from Allah﴾, meaning: "And before this, this is your neglect of Joseph," so "mā" is the subject, and its predicate is "wa-min qabl" (and before). It was also said: "mā" is a connecting particle (ṣila), and the meaning is "and from this, you neglected Joseph," i.e., you fell short and wasted him. It was also said: it is in the nominative as a predicate of a complete sentence.

﴿So I will not leave the land (arḍ) in which I am﴾, which is the land of Egypt, ﴿until my father permits me to leave it, or Allah judges for me﴾ to leave it, and leave my brother Benjamin there or with him; otherwise I will not leave it. Abu Salih said: "or Allah judges for me" with the sword, so that I may fight whoever has imprisoned my brother Benjamin.

﴿And He is the best of judges﴾, the most excellent and most just of those who decide between people.

The other brother, the one detained in Egypt, says this to his brothers: "Return to your father and say: 'O our father, your son Benjamin has stolen the goblet.'" Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak read *suriqa* (سُرِّق) with a ḍammah on the sīn, a kasrah on the rā' and a shaddah, in the passive form without a named agent (*mā lam yusamma fā'iluhu*). The meaning is that he was attributed to theft, like *khawwantuhu* (I accused him of betrayal) and *fajjartuhu* (I attributed immorality to him). That is, he was ascribed these qualities. [....]

"We bear witness only to what we know": this means that we never gave testimony at any time in our lives except to what we knew. This is not a testimony from us; rather, it is a report of the conduct of your son according to their claim. Ibn Ishaq said: its meaning is, "We only said that he stole because of what we knew." He said: the judgment among the prophets, Ya'qub and his sons, was that a thief should be enslaved for his theft.

"And we were not guardians of the unseen": Mujahid and Qatadah said: we did not know that your son would steal and that our affair would come to this. Had we known that, we would not have taken him with us. We only said, "We will guard our brother against what we have no means of guarding him against." Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, said: they meant that he stole at night while they were asleep, and that *al-ghayb* (the unseen) means the night in the language of Himyar. Ibn 'Abbas said: we did not know what he did by night or by day, or his coming and going. 'Ikrimah said: "And we were not guardians of the unseen" means: perhaps it was planted in his baggage at night.

It was also said that its meaning is: the theft was taken from his baggage while we were watching him, and we have no knowledge of the unseen; so perhaps they stole it and he did not steal. This is the meaning of the saying of Abu Ishaq. Ibn Kaysan said: we did not know that you would be afflicted as you were afflicted with Yusuf, and had we known that, we would not have taken your son and would not have gone away with him.

"And ask the town in which we were": that is, the people of the town, which is Egypt. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is a town among the towns of Egypt.

"And the caravan in which we came": that is, the caravan in which we were. There were with them people from Canaan, neighbours of Ya'qub (peace be upon him). Ibn Ishaq said: the brother detained in Egypt knew that his brothers were suspected by their father because of what they had done concerning his affair, so he instructed them to say this statement. "And indeed we are truthful."

He said: "Rather, your souls have made a matter attractive to you" — the verse is abridged in meaning. They returned to their father and told him that. He said: "Rather, your souls have made attractive to you a matter you desired." "So patience is beautiful. It may be that Allah will bring them all to me": Yusuf, Benjamin and their brother who remains in Egypt. "Indeed He is the All-Knowing of my grief and my longing over their loss, the All-Wise in the management of His creation."

They said: ﴿We miss the goblet of the king﴾. The reciters differed over how this is recited. Qathm narrated from Dawud ibn Abi Hind, from a client of the Banu Hashim, from Abu Hurayra that he recited ṣā' al-malik (صاع الملك). Abu Raja' recited ṣawʿ (صوع), and Yahya ibn Ma'mar recited ṣawgh (صوغ) with a ghayn. [It is said that] it is derived from ṣāgha, yaṣūghu, ṣawgh, and the plural of ṣawā' (صواع) is ṣiyaʿ, while the plural of ṣāʿ is aṣwāʿ.

﴿And for him who brings it, a camel's load [of grain]﴾, ﴿and I am its guarantor (zaʿīm)﴾. Zaʿīm means a guarantor, as the caller (mu'adhdhin) says. The root sense of zaʿīm is one who takes charge of a people's affairs, and a leader is also called zaʿīm. One says zaʿama, zaʿāma, and ziʿāman. Layla al-Akhyaliyya said:

"Until, when the banner was raised, I saw him
Beneath the banner, over the army, as a leader (zaʿīm)."

[Kitab al-'Ayn: 1/364.]

﴿They said﴾, meaning the brothers of Joseph: ﴿By Allah (tallāhi)﴾, i.e., ﴿wallāhi﴾. Its original is the letter waw, which was changed into tā', as the reciters did in taqwā, tukalān, turāb and tukhma. Its original is waw, and the waw in all these words is part of the noun, but in tallāhi it is not so, since it is only the waw of oath. The [Arab] usage became common on their tongues, and they considered the waw to be part of the letter itself, so they changed it into tā'. It was placed in this one word only, not in the other names of Allah, exalted is He.

﴿Indeed you know that we came not to cause corruption in the land, and we were not thieves﴾. If it is asked: from where did they know this?

The answer: al-Kalbi said that Joseph's servant, who was the caller (mu'adhdhin), said to them: "The king entrusted me with the goblet, and I fear the king's punishment. Today I have a good word to say to him. If I do not find it, I fear that my standing will fall and I will be disgraced in Egypt." They said: ﴿Indeed you know that we came not to cause corruption in the land﴾. Since we set out on this road we have not stayed with anyone, nor have we corrupted anything. Ask about us those whom we passed by: did we harm anyone, or did we spoil anything? We have also returned the money that we found in our saddlebags. If we were thieves, we would not have returned it.

Joseph's servant said: "It is the great goblet of the king, with which he measures." Some of them said: they only said that because they were known not to take what was not theirs. It was also said: when they entered Egypt they covered the mouths of their animals so that they would not eat from people's fields.

If it is asked: how did Joseph permit calling them thieves? It is answered that there are two answers. One is that he concealed in himself that they had stolen him from his father. The other is that it was the speech of the caller, not an order from Joseph, and Allah knows best.

﴿They said﴾, meaning the caller and his companions: ﴿What then shall be its penalty﴾, i.e., its recompense. Al-Akhfash said: if you wish, you may return the pronoun to the thieves, and if you wish, to the theft ﴿if you are liars﴾ in your saying: ﴿we were not thieves﴾.

They said: ﴿Its penalty is that he in whose saddlebag it is found, he himself shall be its penalty﴾, that the stolen property be handed over to the one from whom it was stolen, and he shall be enslaved for a year. This was the custom of the family of Jacob concerning the judgment for a thief. ﴿Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers﴾, those who do what is not theirs to do, by taking another's property through theft.

As for the grammatical construction, al-Farra' said: "man" (he who) is in the sense of "jazā'uhu" (its penalty). The meaning of man is raised by the pronoun that comes after it, and the answer of the conditional is the fa' in His saying ﴿fa-huwa jazā'uhu﴾ (then he himself is its penalty). The second "jazā'uhu" is raised by the implied meaning of the conditional and its answer. A similar usage in speech is when someone says: "What is due to me from you?" and the other replies: "For you from me is that, if you give me good news, you will have a thousand dirhams." It is as if he said: "For you from me is this." If you wish, the penalty may be raised by "man" alone and its relative clause, as if you said: "Its penalty is the one found in his saddlebag," as if you said: "Its recompense is that he be enslaved [in the future] also," so he said: ﴿fa-huwa jazā'uhu﴾. The summary of these sayings is: its penalty is the penalty of the one found in his saddlebag, or its penalty is the one found in his saddlebag. The sentence is complete.

He began with ﴿fa-huwa jazā'uhu﴾ and then the messenger said: "It is necessary to search your goods; you are not thieves until I search them." He then took them back to Joseph, and ﴿he began with their bags﴾ to remove suspicion, ﴿before the bag of his brother﴾. He had searched their goods one by one. Qatada said: we are told that he would not open any goods or look into any bag without seeking Allah's forgiveness, out of guilt for the accusation he had made against them. Until only the youth remained, he said: "I do not think this one took anything." His brothers said: "By Allah, we will not move until you search his saddlebag, for it is more pleasing to you and to us." When they opened his goods, they extracted it from them. That is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He took it out from his brother's bag﴾. The pronoun in His saying "istakhrajahā" (he extracted it) is feminine, while ṣuwā' (goblet) is masculine. Allah said: ﴿and for him who brings it, a camel's load﴾, because returning it to the water-vessel (al-siqāya) is like His saying: ﴿those who inherit the Firdaws﴾, then He said: ﴿therein they will abide forever﴾ [Qur'an 23:11], returning the pronoun to Paradise. And His saying:

"When the division is attended by the relatives, the orphans, and the needy,"
then He said: ﴿provide for them from it﴾ [Qur'an 4:8], i.e., from the inheritance.

It was also said: the pronoun returns to the theft. It was also said: He made it feminine because ṣuwā' is used as both masculine and feminine. Whoever made it feminine said: "thalāth aṣwuʿ" (three ṣāʿs) like "adūd" (cups), and whoever made it masculine said: "thalātha aṣwāʿ" (three ṣuwā's), like "thalātha athwāb" (three garments).

﴿Thus We devised for Joseph﴾, i.e., just as they acted at the beginning toward Joseph, We acted toward them. Allah related that Jacob said to Joseph: ﴿lest they plot against you a plot﴾ [Qur'an 12:5]. So the plot is the recompense of a plot. Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿thus We devised﴾ means "We did," al-Rabi' said: "We inspired," and Ibn al-Anbari said: "We willed."

The meaning of the verse: thus We acted for Joseph, until he took his brother to himself and separated him from his brothers by a pretext which Allah devised for him, and Joseph used it as a pretext. ﴿He could not have taken his brother in the king's religion﴾, i.e., in the king's judgment and ruling. This was said by Qatada. Ibn 'Abbas said: "in the king's authority." The root of dīn (religion) is obedience. The king's ruling concerning a thief was that he be enslaved, and that he pay double the value of what he stole to the one from whom it was stolen. Al-Dahhak said: when a thief was brought to the king, he would expose his buttocks and blind his eyes. ﴿Unless Allah wills﴾, i.e., Joseph would not have been able to take his brother Benjamin from among his brothers and hold him with him under the king's judgment, had it not been for what We devised for him through Our kindness, until he found the way to that, which was what he caused to be spoken on the tongues of his brothers, that the penalty for a thief is enslavement. So they acknowledged it and showed their willingness to hand over the brother to him. That was the intent of Joseph (peace be upon him). [See Fath al-Qadir: 3/43.]

﴿We raise by degrees whom We will﴾, by knowledge, just as We raised Joseph above his brothers.

﴿And above every possessor of knowledge is one who knows﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: this one is more knowing than that one, and that one is more knowing than this one, and Allah is above every knower. Qatada and al-Hasan said: by Allah, there is no scholar on the face of the earth but that above him is one more knowing than he, until knowledge reaches Allah, who taught it, and from Him it began and to Him it returns. In the recitation of 'Abd Allah it is: "wa fawqa kulli dhī ʿilmin ʿalīm" (and above every knower is one who knows).

It is narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi that 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah honor his face, gave a judgment in a case, and a man from the side of the mosque said: "O Commander of the Faithful, the judgment is not as you have judged." He said: "Then what is it?" He said: "Such and such." He said: "You are right and you are wrong!!" ﴿And above every possessor of knowledge is one who knows﴾.

They said: When the goblet was taken out of Benjamin's saddlebag, his brothers lowered their heads out of shame and turned to Benjamin and said: "O Benjamin, what is this that you have done? You have disgraced us and blackened our faces. O sons of Rachel, you are never free of trouble from us. When did you take the goblet?"

Benjamin said: "Rather, the sons of Rachel are those from whom you are never free of trouble. You took my brother and destroyed him in the wilderness. This goblet was placed in my saddlebag by the one who placed the dirhams in your saddlebags."

Then they said to Joseph: ﴿If he steals, a brother of his has stolen before﴾, i.e., from his father and mother, before. Scholars differed about the theft with which they charged Joseph. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatada said: Joseph stole an idol belonging to his maternal grandfather, broke it, and threw it on the road. Al-Kalbi said: his mother sent him when she wanted to leave Haran with Jacob for Palestine and Jordan. She ordered him to go and take a jar in which there were idols belonging to her son, so that when his father missed them he would become Muslim. He went, took it, and brought it to his mother. This is the theft they mean.

It is narrated from Ibn Juraij: Joseph's mother ordered him to steal an idol belonging to his maternal uncle which he worshipped, and she was a Muslim. Abu Kurayb narrated from Abu Idris who said: I heard my father say: the children of Jacob were at a meal, and Joseph looked at a bone (ʿirq), and hid it, so they reproached him for that. 'Abd Allah ibn al-Sadi narrated, from his father, from Mujahid, that a beggar came to the house, and Joseph stole a [garment] from the house and gave it to the beggar, so they reproached him for it. Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna said: Joseph stole a hen from among the birds that were in Jacob's house and gave it to a beggar.

Ka'b said: Joseph was alone in the house, and a beggar came to him, and in the house there was an ʿatāq (a female young goat), and he gave it to the beggar without his father's order. Wahb said: he used to set aside food from the table for the poor.

Hisham narrated from Sa'd ibn Zayd ibn Aslam concerning this verse: Joseph (peace be upon him) was with his mother at the house of a maternal uncle of his. He entered while he was a child playing, and took a small golden statue. That is the reproach of his brothers to him.

Ibn Ishaq narrated from Mujahid, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, who said: the first trial that befell Joseph, as it has reached me, was that his paternal aunt, the daughter of Isaac, who was the eldest of Isaac's children, had Isaac's girdle (mintaqa). They used to inherit it by seniority from their in-laws, and whoever held it had a sort of sovereignty that could not be contested, so he could do with it as he wished. Rachel, Joseph's mother, had died, so his aunt raised him and loved him intensely, and could not bear to be parted from him.

When he grew up and reached years of age, Jacob's love for him became strong. Jacob came to her and said: "O sister, hand Joseph over to me, for by Allah I cannot bear for him to be absent from me for an hour." She said: "No." He said: "By Allah, I will not leave him." She said: "Leave him with me for some days, that I may look at him, perhaps that will console me for him." He did so. When Jacob had left her, she took Isaac's girdle and tied it around Joseph beneath his clothes while he was young. Then she said: "The girdle of Isaac has been lost. Search for whoever took it." They searched but it was not found. She said: "Examine the people of the house." They examined them, and it was found with Joseph. She said: "By Allah, he is my bondsman; I may do with him as I wish." Jacob came to her and she told him the news. He said: "If he did that, then he is your bondsman. I can do nothing else." So she kept him, and Jacob could do nothing for him until she died. This is what Joseph's brothers meant when they said: ﴿If he steals, a brother of his has stolen before﴾, and this is the well-known proverb: "His excuse is worse than his crime."

﴿So Joseph kept it secret within himself﴾, he concealed it, ﴿and did not reveal it to them﴾. He used the feminine pronoun because he meant by it the word and the saying, and this is a recitation.

He said: ﴿You are worse in position﴾, i.e., worse in standing with Allah, than those whom you accuse of theft, in your conduct toward Joseph. ﴿And Allah knows best what you describe﴾, you say. Qatada said: "what you lie about."

The narrators said: When they entered upon Joseph, and the goblet was extracted from Benjamin's saddlebag, Joseph called for the goblet, struck it, and brought it close to his ear, then said: "Indeed, this goblet of mine informs me that you were twelve men, and that you set out with a brother of yours and sold him." When Benjamin heard this, he stood up and prostrated to Joseph, then said: "O King, ask your goblet of this brother of mine, where he is." He struck it and said: "Is he alive? You will see him." Benjamin said: "Do with me as you wish, for if he knows about me, he will rescue me." Joseph entered and wept, then performed ablution and came out. Benjamin said: "O King, I think you should strike your goblet, and it will tell you the truth about who stole it and placed it in my saddlebag." He struck it and said: "Indeed, this goblet of mine has disobeyed me, and it says: 'How do you ask me about my companion, when you have seen with whom you were?'"

He said: When the sons of Jacob grew angry, they could not be restrained. Rubayl grew angry and said: "By Allah, O King, either you release us, or I will cry out a cry that will leave no pregnant woman in Egypt without miscarrying what is in her womb." Every hair on Rubayl's body stood up, and he trembled from [......] [[unreadable word.]] Joseph touched him and his anger subsided. Rubayl said: "Who is this? In this land there is surely a seed from the seed of Jacob."

Joseph said: "And who is Jacob?" Rubayl became angry and said: "O King, do not mention Jacob, for he is the chosen one (sirr) of Allah, son of the sacrificed one (dhabīḥ) of Allah, son of the intimate friend (khalīl) of the Most Merciful." Joseph said: [Bear witness] if you are truthful.

Joseph held his brother, and by the judgment of his brothers he had more right to him than they did. They saw that there was no way to free him except by asking him to release him in exchange for something they would give him. ﴿They said: O Chief, indeed he has an aged father, [who is attached to his love]﴾, meaning Jacob. ﴿So take one of us in his place﴾, as a substitute. ﴿Indeed, we see you as one of the good-doers﴾ in your conduct. It was said: toward us. Ibn Ishaq said: they meant that if you do that, you will be among the good-doers.

He said: ﴿Allah forbid﴾, I seek refuge in Allah. It is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), and so the Arabs do with every verbal noun that stands in place of the verb. They say: "ḥamdan lillāh" (praise to Allah) and "shukran lillāh" (thanks to Allah), meaning "aḥmad Allāh" and "ashkuruh." ﴿That we should take only him with whom we found our property﴾, and he did not say "the one who stole," out of caution against lying. ﴿Indeed, then we would be wrongdoers﴾, if we took an innocent person for a guilty one.

﴿So when they despaired of him﴾, meaning they despaired of Joseph that he would answer what they asked, ﴿they withdrew to confer privately (najiyyan)﴾, i.e., they were alone with one another, consulting and conferring, with no others mixing with them. Najī is used for a group that confers, and it may also apply to one person. Allah said of one person: ﴿and We brought him near as a confidant (najiyyan)﴾ [Qur'an 19:52], and of the plural: ﴿they withdrew to confer privately (najiyyan)﴾. It is permissible for both the singular and the plural because it is a verbal noun used as an adjective, like "ʿadl" (justice), "zūr" (falsehood), "fiṭr" and the like. It derives from the saying: "najawtu fulānan anjūhu najiyyan" (I conferred with so-and-so privately). Similarly "najwā" is both a noun and a verbal noun. Allah said: ﴿and when they were in confidential talk (najwā)﴾ [Qur'an 17:47], i.e., conferring. He said: ﴿There is no private conference (najwā) of three﴾ [Qur'an 58:7], and of the verbal noun: ﴿Private conference is only from Satan﴾ [Qur'an 58:10]. A poet said:

"Banī Badā, the secret talk of men (khabb najwā al-rijāl),
(and) in your confidence be like the confidant's secret talk (khabb al-najiyy)."

In this verse, najwā and najiyy mean "consultation." The plural of najiyy is anjiya. Labid said:

"I witnessed the confidants of the stance (anjiyyat al-ifāqa), exalted,
My heels and the buttocks of the kings were witnesses."

Another said:

"Indeed, when the people are confidants (anjiya),
and their necks are shaking like ropes of a well-bucket,
there, advise me, and do not advise anyone else about him."

﴿The eldest of them said﴾, meaning in intellect and knowledge, not in age. He was Simeon (Shim'ūn), and he was their leader. This was said by Mujahid. Qatada, al-Suddi, al-Dahhak and Ka'b said: he was Rubayl, who was the oldest of them, and he was the cousin (son of the maternal aunt) of Joseph, and he was the one who forbade his brothers from killing him. Wahb and al-Kalbi said: Judah (Yahudha), who was the most intelligent of them. Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: Levi (Lāwī).

﴿Did you not know that your father took from you a solemn pledge (mawthiq) from Allah﴾, a covenant from Allah. ﴿And before this you neglected Joseph﴾. Scholars differed about the grammatical position of "mā" (what). Some said: it is in the accusative, governed by the verb of knowing, meaning: "Did you not know that before this, you neglected Joseph?" Others said: it is in the nominative, as the subject of a sentence, and the sentence is complete at His saying: ﴿from Allah﴾, meaning: "And before this, this is your neglect of Joseph," so "mā" is the subject, and its predicate is "wa-min qabl" (and before). It was also said: "mā" is a connecting particle (ṣila), and the meaning is "and from this, you neglected Joseph," i.e., you fell short and wasted him. It was also said: it is in the nominative as a predicate of a complete sentence.

﴿So I will not leave the land (arḍ) in which I am﴾, which is the land of Egypt, ﴿until my father permits me to leave it, or Allah judges for me﴾ to leave it, and leave my brother Benjamin there or with him; otherwise I will not leave it. Abu Salih said: "or Allah judges for me" with the sword, so that I may fight whoever has imprisoned my brother Benjamin.

﴿And He is the best of judges﴾, the most excellent and most just of those who decide between people.

The other brother, the one detained in Egypt, says this to his brothers: "Return to your father and say: 'O our father, your son Benjamin has stolen the goblet.'" Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak read *suriqa* (سُرِّق) with a ḍammah on the sīn, a kasrah on the rā' and a shaddah, in the passive form without a named agent (*mā lam yusamma fā'iluhu*). The meaning is that he was attributed to theft, like *khawwantuhu* (I accused him of betrayal) and *fajjartuhu* (I attributed immorality to him). That is, he was ascribed these qualities. [....]

"We bear witness only to what we know": this means that we never gave testimony at any time in our lives except to what we knew. This is not a testimony from us; rather, it is a report of the conduct of your son according to their claim. Ibn Ishaq said: its meaning is, "We only said that he stole because of what we knew." He said: the judgment among the prophets, Ya'qub and his sons, was that a thief should be enslaved for his theft.

"And we were not guardians of the unseen": Mujahid and Qatadah said: we did not know that your son would steal and that our affair would come to this. Had we known that, we would not have taken him with us. We only said, "We will guard our brother against what we have no means of guarding him against." Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, said: they meant that he stole at night while they were asleep, and that *al-ghayb* (the unseen) means the night in the language of Himyar. Ibn 'Abbas said: we did not know what he did by night or by day, or his coming and going. 'Ikrimah said: "And we were not guardians of the unseen" means: perhaps it was planted in his baggage at night.

It was also said that its meaning is: the theft was taken from his baggage while we were watching him, and we have no knowledge of the unseen; so perhaps they stole it and he did not steal. This is the meaning of the saying of Abu Ishaq. Ibn Kaysan said: we did not know that you would be afflicted as you were afflicted with Yusuf, and had we known that, we would not have taken your son and would not have gone away with him.

"And ask the town in which we were": that is, the people of the town, which is Egypt. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is a town among the towns of Egypt.

"And the caravan in which we came": that is, the caravan in which we were. There were with them people from Canaan, neighbours of Ya'qub (peace be upon him). Ibn Ishaq said: the brother detained in Egypt knew that his brothers were suspected by their father because of what they had done concerning his affair, so he instructed them to say this statement. "And indeed we are truthful."

He said: "Rather, your souls have made a matter attractive to you" — the verse is abridged in meaning. They returned to their father and told him that.
