As for me, I had a son who was the dearest of my children to me, and his brothers took him to the wilderness, then brought me his shirt stained with blood and said: 'The wolf has eaten him.' [..........] [[an illegible word.]] Then I had another son, who was his full brother, and I was consoled by him; they took him, then returned and said: 'He has stolen, and you have imprisoned him for it. We are a household that does not steal and does not bear a thief. If you return him to me, well and good; otherwise I will call down a curse upon you that will reach the seventh of your descendants.'" When Yusuf read the letter, he could not restrain his weeping, his patience gave way, and he said that to them.

Some said: he said it when he asked his brother Binyamin: "Do you have a son?" He said: "Yes, three sons." He said: "What did you name them?" He said: "I named the eldest Yusuf." He said: "Why?" He said: "Out of love for you, to remember you by him." He said: "What did you name the second?" He said: "Dhi'b (wolf)." He said: "Why did you name him after the wolf, when it is a savage beast?" He said: "To remember you by him." He said: "What did you name the third?" He said: "Dimaa' (blood)." He said: "Why?" He said: "To remember you by him." When Yusuf heard the words, the tears choked him and he could not restrain himself; he said to his brothers when they had come in to him: ﴿Do you know what you did to Yusuf and his brother, when you separated them and did what you did, when you were ignorant?﴾ — about what Yusuf's affair would come to.

It is also said: the wrongdoer is ignorant at the time of his wrongdoing.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "when you were children." al-Hasan said: "when you were young men." This is not far from the truth, because youth is the time when ignorance is expected.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 12, verses 84–93 (part 2 of 2):

If it is asked about the meaning of Yusuf's words ﴿What did you do to Yusuf and his brother?﴾, and it is said: how could he address them about his brother when they had not striven to imprison him? The answer is that when they spoke freely against their brother on account of the cup, [and imprisoned him], saying: "We have not seen anything from you, O sons of Rahil," as we have mentioned, Yusuf rebuked them for that. It is also said: since the two were from one mother, and they used to harm him after the loss of Yusuf, he rebuked them for that.

﴿They said: "Are you indeed Yusuf?"﴾ Ibn Muhsin and Ibn Kathir read: "Innaka" as a declarative statement, while the others read it as an interrogative. Their evidence is the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "Aw anta Yusuf" (or you are Yusuf). Ibn Ishaq said: When Yusuf said to his brothers, ﴿Do you know what you did to Yusuf and his brother?﴾ up to the end of the verse, the veil was lifted from them and the screen was removed, so they recognized him and said: ﴿Indeed, are you Yusuf?﴾. Juwaybir reported from al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas, who said: Yusuf said, "Do you know what you did to Yusuf?" Then he smiled, and when he smiled, his front teeth were like strung pearls. When they saw his front teeth, they likened him to Yusuf, and so they said to him, interrogatively: ﴿Are you indeed Yusuf?﴾. Ibn Sam'an reported from Ata' from Ibn Abbas, who said: The brothers of Yusuf did not recognize him until the crown was removed from him. On his forehead there was a mark, and Ya'qub had a similar mark, Ishaq had a similar mark, and Sarah had a similar mark, resembling a white birthmark. When he said to them, ﴿Do you know what you did to Yusuf and his brother?﴾ and removed the crown from himself, they recognized him and said: ﴿Are you indeed Yusuf?﴾ [Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 9/256].

He said: ﴿I am Yusuf, and this is my brother. Allah has been gracious to us by bringing us together after you had separated us.﴾ ﴿Indeed, whoever fears Allah, by performing His obligations and avoiding His prohibitions, and is patient over what Allah has forbidden him,﴾ Ibn Abbas said: ﴿fears Allah﴾ refers to fornication, and ﴿is patient﴾ refers to remaining chaste; Mujahid said: ﴿fears the disobedience of Allah and is patient over prison﴾. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not waste the reward of the good-doers.﴾

Then they said, acknowledging and apologizing: ﴿By Allah, Allah has certainly preferred you over us﴾, meaning Allah has chosen you over us in knowledge, wisdom, intellect, virtue, beauty, and kingship. ﴿And we were indeed sinners﴾, meaning we were indeed sinful and wrongdoers in our conduct toward you. It is said: "khati'a, yakhta'u, khata'an and akhta'a" when one commits a sin. Umayyah ibn al-Akshar said:
"Indeed, two emigrants who surrounded him, by the Lord's life, have erred and failed."
[Jami' al-Bayan of al-Tabari: 13/73; in it, "khaba" is given instead of "khaba."]

It was said to Ibn Abbas: How did they say, ﴿We were sinners﴾, when they had deliberately intended that? He said: They erred regarding the truth even though they intended it, and everyone who commits a sin in this way strays from the path of truth that is upon him, until he falls into doubt and disobedience. Then Yusuf, who was forbearing and granted success, said: ﴿No reproach shall be upon you today﴾, meaning no rebuke or reproach upon you, and I will not mention your sin to you after today. The root of "tathrib" is corruption, and it is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz. From it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "If the slave-girl of one of you commits fornication, let him flog her with the prescribed punishment and not reproach her" [Kanz al-Ummal: 5/338, no. 13116], meaning he should not shame her. Then Yusuf prayed for them and said: ﴿May Allah forgive you, and He is the Most Merciful of the merciful.﴾

Ata' reported from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Prophet ﷺ took hold of the two door-posts on the day of the conquest of Makkah while people had taken refuge in the House, and said: "Praise be to Allah, who fulfilled His promise, helped His servant, and defeated the confederates alone" [Musnad Ahmad: 2/11; Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 9/258]. Then he said: "What do you think?" [In the source: "What do you think, O assembly of Quraysh?"] They said: "We think good; a noble brother and the son of a noble brother, and you have gained power." He said: "I say as my brother Yusuf said: ﴿No reproach shall be upon you today﴾" [Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 9/256].

Al-Suddi and others said: When Yusuf made himself known to them, he asked them about his father. He said: "What has happened to him?" They said: "His eyes have gone white." So he gave them his shirt and said to them: ﴿Go with this shirt of mine and cast it upon the face of my father; he will return seeing.﴾ That is, he will regain sight, because it was a supplication. Al-Dahhak said: That shirt was woven from the fabric of Paradise. Al-Suddi narrated from his father, from Mujahid, regarding this verse, that he said: Yusuf was too knowledgeable of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to think that his shirt would return sight to Ya'qub; rather, that shirt was the shirt of Ibrahim, which Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, clothed him in the Fire, made of silk from Paradise. Ishaq had clothed him with it, and Ishaq had given it to Ya'qub. Ya'qub folded the shirt, placed it in a case, and hung it around Yusuf's neck because he feared the evil eye for him. Then Jibril (peace be upon him) commanded him: "Send your shirt, for in it is the fragrance of Paradise; it does not touch anyone afflicted or sick without their being cured and healed."

﴿And bring me all your family.﴾

And he turned away from them. That was because, when Ya'qub received news of Binyamin, his grief became complete, his distress reached its height, and his sorrow over Yusuf was renewed. So he turned away from them, and said: ﴿O my sorrow over Yusuf!﴾ Mujahid said: "Alas for me!" And al-Asaf (grief) is intense sorrow and regret.

﴿And his eyes turned white from grief﴾. Muqatil said: he could not see with them for six years. ﴿And he was kazim﴾, that is, makdum, filled with sorrow, restraining it and not disclosing it; from the same root comes kazm al-ghayz (restraining anger). 'Ata al-Khurasani said: kazim means sorrowful. Mujahid said: crushed. al-Dahhak said: stricken. Qatadah said: his sorrow churned within his inner self, and he did not speak evil, nor did he speak except good. Ibn Zayd said: his distress reached the point that he would not speak to them. Ibn 'Abbas said: troubled. Muqatil said: afflicted. All of these are close in meaning.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr reported from Ibn 'Abbas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah did not give any nation ﴿Indeed we belong to Allah and to Him we shall return﴾ at the time of calamity except the nation of Muhammad. Do you not see that Ya'qub, when he was afflicted, did not say it? He only said: ﴿O my sorrow over Yusuf!﴾" [123] [[Jami' al-Bayan of al-Tabari: 13/53; Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 5/444, with variation; it is found in full in al-Tafsir al-Safi of al-Fayd al-Kashani: 3/38.]]

And Ibn Fanjawayh [said: narrated to us Abu Bakr ibn Malik] al-Qati'i, who said: narrated to us 'Abdullah ibn Ahmad ibn Hanbal, [said: narrated to me] my father, from Hisham [ibn al-Qasim], from al-Hasan, who said: Between the time Yusuf left his father's lap and the day he met him there were eighty years, and Ya'qub's eyes never dried; and on the face of the earth there was no one more honoured by Allah than Ya'qub.

﴿They said﴾, meaning the sons of Ya'qub: ﴿By Allah, you will not cease remembering Yusuf﴾, that is, you will not stop remembering Yusuf; you will not slacken in your love for him. It is said: "I did not cease (ma fati'tu) saying that," and "ma fata'a / ma fata' / yaftu," with the root fata'a and fataw. Aws ibn Hajar said:

"So the horses did not cease, while their dust was like a tent on a windy day, rising..." [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 13/55; Lisan al-Arab: 12/322, where it reads: "so the horses did not cease."]]

Another said:

"So the horses did not cease to return and claim, and some of them were overtaken and cut off..." [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 13/55; Zad al-Masir: 4/205.]]

That is, "so they did not cease."

The negation (la) is omitted with the verb fati'a, as in the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"I said: by Allah's oath, I shall not leave sitting, even if they cut off my head and limbs beside you." [[al-Sihah: 6/2222.]]

That is: "I shall not leave."

Khidash ibn Zuhayr said:

"And I shall not leave, as long as Allah keeps my people, by Allah's praise, girded and noble..." [[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 11/9; Lisan al-Arab: 10/354, where it reads "against the enemies" instead of "by Allah's praise."]]

That is: "I shall not leave." And similar examples are many.

﴿Until you become harad﴾. The words of the exegetes differ regarding it. Ibn 'Abbas said: dana (gravely ill). al-'Awfi said: that is, wasted away by illness. Mujahid said: it is what is short of death, meaning close to death. Qatadah said: aged. al-Dahhak said: worn out and having turned his back. Ibn Ishaq said: corrupt, with no benefit in you. Ibn Zayd said: harad is one who has been returned to the lowest point of life until he no longer understands. al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: skin dried over the bone. Muqatil said: gravely ill. al-Kisa'i said: harad is one who is corrupt and has no good in him. al-Akhfash said: meaning gone away. al-Mukhrij said: melting from grief. al-Farra' reported from some: weak, without movement in you. al-Hasan said: like a broken, crushed water-skin. 'Allam said: exhausted and wasted away. Ibn al-Anbari said: perishing, corrupt. al-Qutaybi said: fallen. All of these are close in meaning.

The meaning of the verse: until his body is worn out by illness and his mind is confused. The root of harad is corruption in the body or mind from grief, love, or old age. From it is the saying of al-'Arji:

"I am a man whom love has driven to excess, which has made me harad, until I was worn out and illness wasted me..." [[al-Sihah: 3/107.]]

It is said: a man is harad, a woman is harad, two men or two women are harad, and men or women are harad; the singular, dual, plural, masculine and feminine are alike in this, because it is a verbal noun placed in the position of a noun. Some Arabs say for the male "harid" and for the female "harida"; when described with this word it is made dual, plural and feminine. It is said: harada, yahridu, haradan and haraadah, so he is harad. It is also said: rajul muharrad. He recited on this:

"The horses pursued him for a whole day, and had they overtaken him he would have become muharrad..." [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 13/57.]]

Imru' al-Qays said:

"I see the man with many camels in the morning made harad, like a young camel made sick in the encampments..." [[Lisan al-Arab: 7/134.]]

﴿Or you become of those who perish﴾, that is, the dead.

Ya'qub said at that point, when he saw their harshness and the badness of their speech: ﴿I only complain of my anguish and my grief to Allah﴾, not to you. The exegetes said: a neighbour came to Ya'qub and said: "O Ya'qub, why do I see you so broken and wasted, though you have not reached the age your father reached?" He said: "What has broken me and wasted me is what Allah has afflicted me with, the calamity of Yusuf." So Allah revealed to him: "O Ya'qub, do you complain of Me to My creatures?" He said: "My Lord, it is a sin I committed; forgive me." He said: "I have forgiven you." After that, whenever he was asked, he would say: ﴿I only complain of my anguish and my grief to Allah.﴾

Habib ibn Abi Thabit said: It reached me that Ya'qub grew so old that his eyebrows fell over his eyes, and he would lift them with a cloth. A man said to him: "What has brought you to what I see?" He said: "The length of time and the abundance of sorrows." Then Allah revealed to him: "O Ya'qub, you complain of Me?" He said: "A sin I committed; forgive it for me."

It is reported from 'Abdullah ibn Qumayt, who said: I heard my father say: "It reached us that a man said to Ya'qub (peace be upon him): 'What took away your sight?' He said: 'My grief over Yusuf.' He said: 'What bent your back?' He said: 'My grief over his brother.' So Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed to him: 'O Ya'qub, do you complain of Me? By My might and majesty, if they were both dead I would have brought them out for you so that you could see them. I was only displeased with you because you slaughtered a sheep and a needy man came to you, and you gave him nothing. The dearest of My creatures to Me are the prophets, then the needy. So prepare food and invite the needy to it.' He prepared food and said: 'Whoever is fasting, let him break his fast tonight with the family of Ya'qub.'"

Abu 'Imran reported from Abu al-Khalad and Wahb ibn Munabbih, who both said: Allah the Exalted revealed to Ya'qub: "Do you know why I punished you and kept Yusuf and Binyamin away from you?" He said: "No, my God." He said: "Because you slaughtered fattened lambs and withheld from your neighbour, and you ate and did not feed him." It is also said: the cause of Ya'qub's trial with the loss of Yusuf was that he had a cow with calves, and he slaughtered its calves before its eyes, while it was lowing, and he showed it no mercy; so Allah seized him for it and afflicted him with the loss of Yusuf, his dearest son.

Wahb ibn Munabbih, al-Suddi and others said: Jibril came to Yusuf while he was in prison and said: "Do you know me, O truthful one?" He said: "I see a pure form and a good scent." He said: "I am the messenger of the Lord of the worlds, and I am the trustworthy Spirit." He said: "What has brought you into the prison of the guilty, when you are the best of the good, the chief of those brought near, and the trustee of the Lord of the worlds?" He said: "Do you not know, O Yusuf, that Allah purifies houses for these good people, and that the land you enter is the purest of lands, and that Allah has purified the prison and what is around it through you, O purest of the pure and son of the righteous?"

He said: "How can I be the son of the truthful, when you count me among the sincere, and I have been made to enter the place of the guilty and named with the name of the corrupt?" He said: "Because your heart was not tempted, and you did not obey your mistress in disobeying your Lord; therefore Allah named you among the truthful, counted you with the sincere, and joined you to your righteous fathers." He said: "Do you have any knowledge of Ya'qub, O Trustworthy Spirit?" He said: "Yes. Allah gave him a beautiful trial and afflicted him with grief over you, ﴿so he was kazim﴾." He said: "What is the measure of his grief?" He said: "The grief of seventy bereaved mothers." He said: "What reward does he have, O Jibril?" He said: "The reward of a hundred martyrs." He said: "Do you think I shall meet him?" He said: "Yes." So Yusuf's soul was content, and he said: "I do not mind whatever befalls me, so long as I see him."

As for His saying ﴿anguish﴾: al-bathth is intense grief, so named because its owner cannot bear it until he discloses it, that is, makes it manifest. It is said: baththa, yabuththu, fahuwa bathth, and abatha [yu'bithuhu ab'than] [[Addition to correct the text from Taj al-'Arus: 1/598; the manuscript wording is illegible.]] yabuthu, fahuwa mubathth when he made it manifest. Dhu al-Rummah said:

"I stopped at the abode of Lumayya, my she-camel, and I kept weeping there and addressing it, and I gave it to drink until it nearly spoke to me, its stones and its playgrounds, of what I disclosed..." [[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 9/251; Lisan al-Arab: 14/391, where it reads "I gave its abode to drink" instead of "I wept there."]]

al-Hasan said: al-bathth is my need. Muhammad ibn al-Qasim al-Anbari said: al-bathth is dispersal. Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: its meaning is: "I only complain of my grief which I am in to Allah," and it is from the phrase bathth al-hadith (spreading the report).

﴿I know from Allah what you do not know.﴾

Ibn 'Abbas said: he means, "I know that Yusuf's dream is true, and that I and you will prostrate to him." Others said: "And I know that Yusuf is alive."

al-Suddi said: when his sons told him about the king's conduct and his words, Ya'qub's soul was stirred and he hoped, and said: "Perhaps it is Yusuf." It is also reported that he saw the king in a dream and asked him: "Has the soul of Yusuf been taken?" He said: "No, by Allah, and he is alive."

It is also said: Allah sent a wolf to him, which greeted him and spoke to him. Ya'qub said to it: "Have you eaten my son, the coolness of my eye and the fruit of my heart?" It said: "By Allah, you know, O Ya'qub, that the flesh of prophets and the children of prophets is forbidden to us." That is why he said to his sons: ﴿O my sons, go and search for news of Yusuf and his brother, and do not despair of the mercy of Allah.﴾ "Go and seek the report of Yusuf and his brother." The word tahassassu is from the root hass, meaning: seek out. Ibn 'Abbas said: seek. ﴿And do not despair﴾, that is, do not lose hope; ﴿of the mercy of Allah﴾: of Allah's relief. Ibn Zayd, Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: of Allah's mercy. ﴿Indeed no one despairs of the mercy of Allah except the disbelieving people.﴾

It is said: Ibn 'Abbas was asked about the difference between tajassus and tahassus, and he said: "They are not far from each other, except that tahassus is in good and tajassus is in evil." al-Hasan and Qatadah said: "It has been related to us that the prophet of Allah Ya'qub never faced a trial without his good opinion of Allah coming to him from behind it, and his opinion of Allah never worsened for an hour of night or day."

al-Hasan reported from al-Ahnaf ibn Qays, from Ibn 'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "David said: 'My God, I hear people say: the God of Abraham, Isaac and Ya'qub; so make me the fourth.' He said: 'You are not there. Abraham never gave Me an equal without My choosing him; Isaac gave himself to Me freely; and Ya'qub, throughout all that he went through, did not despair of Yusuf.'" [124] [[al-Durr al-Manthur: 5/281.]]

﴿They said: O Chief, harm has touched us and our family, and we have come with meagre merchandise...﴾

In the verse something is omitted, which is understood from the context. Its reconstruction: they returned to Egypt until they reached it and entered upon Yusuf, and they said to him: "O Chief" (ayyuha al-'Aziz), that is, O king, in the language of Himyar. ﴿Harm has touched us and our family﴾: adversity and hunger. ﴿And we have come with merchandise that is meagre﴾: little, inferior, deficient, unsalable. It is not accepted for any food except from the seller at a discount. The root of izja' is driving and pushing. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Do you not see that Allah drives the clouds?﴾ [[Surah al-Nur: 43.]] al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani said:

"The wind blew from the direction of Dhu Azal, driving with the night from its cold clouds..." [[al-Sarad is the plural of al-sarid: a cold, moist cloud with no water in it.]] [[Lisan al-Arab: 11/13.]]

Hatim al-Ta'i said:

"Let him weep for Milhan, a guest who was destitute, and a widow driving a widow along with the night..." [[Lisan al-Arab: 11/297.]]

Merchandise is called muzjah only because it is not accepted, and it is accepted only by way of tajwiz, that is, by pushing the one who takes it.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i pronounced it with imalah, and the rest pronounced it with full vowels (tafkhim).

The exegetes differed about what this merchandise was. 'Ikrimah reported from Ibn 'Abbas: it was worn-out dirhams, counterfeit, not accepted except at a discount with his consent; that is, it was not accepted for food, since for the price of food only good coin is taken. Ibn Abi Mulaykah: a rope, the torn sack, and the worn-out rope of goods. 'Abdullah ibn al-Harith: the goods of the Bedouins, wool and ghee. al-Kalbi, Muqatil and Ibn Hayyan: turpentine and green seed. Sa'id ibn Jubayr: [few] dirhams. Ibn Ishaq: few, not enough to buy what they used to buy, unless you overlook for us in them, whether they were better or worse. Juwaybir reported from al-Dahhak: sandals and leather. And it was reported from him that it was the flour of the doum palm.

﴿So fill for us the measure﴾, that is, give us with it what you used to give us before at the full, good price; ﴿and be charitable to us﴾, and show us favour with the difference between the good price and the bad, and do not cheat us in the price. This is the saying of most exegetes. Ibn Jurayj and al-Dahhak said: ﴿be charitable to us﴾ by returning our brother to us.

﴿Indeed Allah rewards the charitable.﴾ al-Dahhak said: they did not say, "Indeed Allah will reward you if you give us charity," because they did not know that he was a believer. 'Abd al-Jabbar ibn al-'Ala' said: Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah was asked: "Was charity forbidden to any of the prophets other than our Prophet (ﷺ)?" Sufyan said: "Have you not heard His saying: ﴿So fill for us the measure and be charitable to us﴾?" Sufyan meant that charity was lawful for them, and that it was forbidden only to our Prophet (ﷺ). It is also reported that al-Hasan al-Basri heard a man say: "O Allah, be charitable to me," and he said: "O man, Allah does not give charity; only one who seeks reward gives charity. Say: O Allah, give me, or show me favour."

﴿He said: Do you know what you did to Yusuf and his brother...﴾

The exegetes differed about the reason that moved Yusuf to say this. Ibn Ishaq said: it was mentioned to me that when they spoke to him with these words, his soul overcame him and tenderness took hold of him, and his tears flowed as he wept; then he disclosed to them what he had been concealing, and said: ﴿Do you know what you did to Yusuf and his brother when you were ignorant?﴾

al-Kalbi said: he said that when he recounted to his brothers that Malik ibn Adhar had said: "I found a boy in a well, with such-and-such a condition, and I bought him from a people for a thousand dirhams." They said: "O King, we sold that boy to him." Yusuf was angered by that and ordered them killed, so they were taken away to be killed. Yahudha turned back, saying: "Ya'qub grieved over the loss of one of us until his sight was gone; how would he be if all his sons were killed?" Then they said: "If you do that, send our goods to our father; he is in such-and-such a place." At that, he showed them mercy, wept, and said to them that statement.

Some said: he said it when he read his father's letter to him. When Ya'qub was told, "Your son has stolen," he wrote to him: "From Ya'qub, Israel of Allah, son of Ishaq, the sacrificed one of Allah, son of Ibrahim, the friend of Allah. To proceed: we are a household on whom trials are constantly imposed. As for my grandfather, his hands and feet were bound and he was thrown into the fire, and Allah made it cool and safe for him. As for my father, his hands and feet were bound and a knife was placed on his nape to be slaughtered, but Allah ransomed him. As for me, I had a son who was the dearest of my children to me, and his brothers took him to the wilderness, then brought me his shirt stained with blood and said: 'The wolf has eaten him.' [..........] [[an illegible word.]] Then I had another son, who was his full brother, and I was consoled by him; they took him, then returned and said: 'He has stolen, and you have imprisoned him for it. We are a household that does not steal and does not bear a thief. If you return him to me, well and good; otherwise I will call down a curse upon you that will reach the seventh of your descendants.'" When Yusuf read the letter, he could not restrain his weeping, his patience gave way, and he said that to them.

Some said: he said it when he asked his brother Binyamin: "Do you have a son?" He said: "Yes, three sons." He said: "What did you name them?" He said: "I named the eldest Yusuf." He said: "Why?" He said: "Out of love for you, to remember you by him." He said: "What did you name the second?" He said: "Dhi'b (wolf)." He said: "Why did you name him after the wolf, when it is a savage beast?" He said: "To remember you by him." He said: "What did you name the third?" He said: "Dimaa' (blood)." He said: "Why?" He said: "To remember you by him." When Yusuf heard the words, the tears choked him and he could not restrain himself; he said to his brothers when they had come in to him: ﴿Do you know what you did to Yusuf and his brother, when you separated them and did what you did, when you were ignorant?﴾ — about what Yusuf's affair would come to.

It is also said: the wrongdoer is ignorant at the time of his wrongdoing.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "when you were children." al-Hasan said: "when you were young men." This is not far from the truth, because youth is the time when ignorance is expected.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 12, verses 84–93 (part 2 of 2):

If it is asked about the meaning of Yusuf's words ﴿What did you do to Yusuf and his brother?﴾, and it is said: how could he address them about his brother when they had not striven to imprison him? The answer is that when they spoke freely against their brother on account of the cup, [and imprisoned him], saying: "We have not seen anything from you, O sons of Rahil," as we have mentioned, Yusuf rebuked them for that. It is also said: since the two were from one mother, and they used to harm him after the loss of Yusuf, he rebuked them for that.

﴿They said: "Are you indeed Yusuf?"﴾ Ibn Muhsin and Ibn Kathir read: "Innaka" as a declarative statement, while the others read it as an interrogative. Their evidence is the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "Aw anta Yusuf" (or you are Yusuf). Ibn Ishaq said: When Yusuf said to his brothers, ﴿Do you know what you did to Yusuf and his brother?﴾ up to the end of the verse, the veil was lifted from them and the screen was removed, so they recognized him and said: ﴿Indeed, are you Yusuf?﴾. Juwaybir reported from al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas, who said: Yusuf said, "Do you know what you did to Yusuf?" Then he smiled, and when he smiled, his front teeth were like strung pearls. When they saw his front teeth, they likened him to Yusuf, and so they said to him, interrogatively: ﴿Are you indeed Yusuf?﴾. Ibn Sam'an reported from Ata' from Ibn Abbas, who said: The brothers of Yusuf did not recognize him until the crown was removed from him. On his forehead there was a mark, and Ya'qub had a similar mark, Ishaq had a similar mark, and Sarah had a similar mark, resembling a white birthmark. When he said to them, ﴿Do you know what you did to Yusuf and his brother?﴾ and removed the crown from himself, they recognized him and said: ﴿Are you indeed Yusuf?﴾ [Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 9/256].

He said: ﴿I am Yusuf, and this is my brother. Allah has been gracious to us by bringing us together after you had separated us.﴾ ﴿Indeed, whoever fears Allah, by performing His obligations and avoiding His prohibitions, and is patient over what Allah has forbidden him,﴾ Ibn Abbas said: ﴿fears Allah﴾ refers to fornication, and ﴿is patient﴾ refers to remaining chaste; Mujahid said: ﴿fears the disobedience of Allah and is patient over prison﴾. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not waste the reward of the good-doers.﴾

Then they said, acknowledging and apologizing: ﴿By Allah, Allah has certainly preferred you over us﴾, meaning Allah has chosen you over us in knowledge, wisdom, intellect, virtue, beauty, and kingship. ﴿And we were indeed sinners﴾, meaning we were indeed sinful and wrongdoers in our conduct toward you. It is said: "khati'a, yakhta'u, khata'an and akhta'a" when one commits a sin. Umayyah ibn al-Akshar said:
"Indeed, two emigrants who surrounded him, by the Lord's life, have erred and failed."
[Jami' al-Bayan of al-Tabari: 13/73; in it, "khaba" is given instead of "khaba."]

It was said to Ibn Abbas: How did they say, ﴿We were sinners﴾, when they had deliberately intended that? He said: They erred regarding the truth even though they intended it, and everyone who commits a sin in this way strays from the path of truth that is upon him, until he falls into doubt and disobedience. Then Yusuf, who was forbearing and granted success, said: ﴿No reproach shall be upon you today﴾, meaning no rebuke or reproach upon you, and I will not mention your sin to you after today. The root of "tathrib" is corruption, and it is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz. From it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "If the slave-girl of one of you commits fornication, let him flog her with the prescribed punishment and not reproach her" [Kanz al-Ummal: 5/338, no. 13116], meaning he should not shame her. Then Yusuf prayed for them and said: ﴿May Allah forgive you, and He is the Most Merciful of the merciful.﴾

Ata' reported from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Prophet ﷺ took hold of the two door-posts on the day of the conquest of Makkah while people had taken refuge in the House, and said: "Praise be to Allah, who fulfilled His promise, helped His servant, and defeated the confederates alone" [Musnad Ahmad: 2/11; Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 9/258]. Then he said: "What do you think?" [In the source: "What do you think, O assembly of Quraysh?"] They said: "We think good; a noble brother and the son of a noble brother, and you have gained power." He said: "I say as my brother Yusuf said: ﴿No reproach shall be upon you today﴾" [Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 9/256].

Al-Suddi and others said: When Yusuf made himself known to them, he asked them about his father. He said: "What has happened to him?" They said: "His eyes have gone white." So he gave them his shirt and said to them: ﴿Go with this shirt of mine and cast it upon the face of my father; he will return seeing.﴾ That is, he will regain sight, because it was a supplication. Al-Dahhak said: That shirt was woven from the fabric of Paradise. Al-Suddi narrated from his father, from Mujahid, regarding this verse, that he said: Yusuf was too knowledgeable of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to think that his shirt would return sight to Ya'qub; rather, that shirt was the shirt of Ibrahim, which Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, clothed him in the Fire, made of silk from Paradise. Ishaq had clothed him with it, and Ishaq had given it to Ya'qub. Ya'qub folded the shirt, placed it in a case, and hung it around Yusuf's neck because he feared the evil eye for him. Then Jibril (peace be upon him) commanded him: "Send your shirt, for in it is the fragrance of Paradise; it does not touch anyone afflicted or sick without their being cured and healed."

﴿And bring me all your family.﴾

When the caravan departed (that is, went out from the outskirts of Egypt heading toward Canaan), their father said: "Indeed, I sense the scent of Joseph" (it is narrated that the wind asked its Lord for permission to bring Jacob the scent of Joseph before the bearer of good news came to him; permission was granted, and it brought it to him). Ibn al-Suddi related from his father, from Mujahid, who said: Jacob caught the scent of Joseph from a distance of three days, because when the wind blew it stirred the shirt and carried the scent of the shirt to Jacob; he found the scent of Paradise, and knew that there is no scent of Paradise on earth except that it comes from that shirt. Therefore he said: "Indeed I sense the scent of Joseph," and he was eight nights' journey away from him.

Shu'bah related from Abu Sinan, who said: I heard Abdullah ibn Abi al-Hudhayl say: I heard Ibn 'Abbas say: Jacob found the scent of Joseph while he was eight nights' journey away from him. Abu Sinan related from Abu Hudhayl, who said: I heard Ibn 'Abbas say: Jacob found the scent of Joseph, and he was eight nights' journey away from him. Shu'bah related from Abu Sinan, who said: I heard Abdullah ibn Abi al-Hudhayl, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning this verse, say: He found its scent from a distance equal to that between Basra and Kufa. Al-Hasan said: It was mentioned to us that between them at that time there were eighty farsakhs.

﴿Unless you think me senile﴾ — Sufyan related from Husayf, from Mujahid, concerning "Unless you think me senile" (la wa-la an tufannidun), he said: "you consider the opinion foolish." From Ibn 'Abbas: "you consider me ignorant." Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Abi Najih related from Mujahid: "lest you say, 'your mind has gone.'" Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Suddi and al-Dahhak said: "you deem me a liar," which is the narration of al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: "you think me senile," and similarly Israil related from Abu Yahya from Mujahid. Al-Rabi' said: "you consider me a fool." Juwaybir related from al-Dahhak: "you think me senile, so you say: 'an old man who has become senile and lost his mind.'" Ibn Yasar said: "you deem me weak." Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: "you find me repugnant." Al-Kisa'i said: "you deem me incapable." Al-Akhfash said: "you blame me." Abu 'Ubaydah said: "you deem me astray."

The root of tafnid (fannada) is corruption. Al-Nabighah said:
"Except Solomon, when the King said to him: 'Stand in the land and restrain it from tafnid.'"
That is, prevent it from corruption. Hence it is said that blame is tafnid. A poet said:
"O my two companions, leave off my blame and my tafnid; what has passed of a matter cannot be returned."
Jarir ibn 'Atiyyah said:
"O my blamers, leave off reproach and be brief; love has lasted long, and you have prolonged tafnid."
Another said:
"You destroyed me with blame and tafnid."
Al-fand is error in speech and opinion. It is said: afnada fulanan al-dahr, meaning when time corrupted him. From the words of Ibn Muqbil:
"Leave time to do what it wills, for when it charges the people with corruption, it corrupts them."

They said — that is, his grandchildren: ﴿By God, you are surely in your old error﴾, your ancient mistake of loving Joseph and not forgetting him.

﴿Then when the bearer of good news came﴾, the one who brought the message of Joseph. Ibn 'Abbas said: the messenger was Yahudha ibn Ya'qub. Ibn Mas'ud said: "the bearer of good news came from ahead of the caravan." Al-Suddi said: Yahudha said: "I was the one who took the shirt stained with blood to Jacob and told him that Joseph had been eaten by the wolf; today I will take the shirt and tell him he is alive, and gladden him as I saddened him." Ibn 'Abbas said: Yahudha carried it alone, apart from them; he went out bareheaded and barefoot and began to run until he reached his father. He had seven loaves with him, which he had not finished eating, and the distance was eighty farsakhs. Al-Dahhak related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: the bearer of good news was Malik ibn Dhu'r from the people of Madyan.

﴿He cast it﴾, that is, the bearer of good news cast Joseph's shirt over Jacob's face, ﴿and he regained his sight﴾: he returned seeing after having been blind.

'Abdullah ibn Ahmad ibn Hanbal related from Abu 'Abdullah al-Sulami, who said: I heard Yahya ibn Muslim, from someone he named, say: Jacob was the most honored of the people of the earth before the Angel of Death, and the Angel of Death asked his Lord for permission to come to Jacob, and was permitted. He came to him, and Jacob said: "O Angel of Death, I ask you by the One who created you: have you taken the soul of Joseph among those you have seized?" He said: "No." The Angel of Death said: "O Jacob, shall I teach you a supplication?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Say: O Possessor of the kindness that never ends and which no one but You can count." So Jacob supplicated with it that night, and the dawn had not risen before he cast the shirt over his face, and he regained his sight. Al-Dahhak said: his sight returned to him after blindness, strength after weakness, youth after decrepitude, and joy after sorrow.

He said: ﴿Did I not tell you that I know from God what you do not know﴾, concerning Joseph's life and that God would reunite us. They said, after that: ﴿O our father, ask forgiveness for us for our sins; indeed we have been sinners﴾, those who were at fault.

Jacob (upon him peace) said: ﴿I will ask my Lord to forgive you﴾ in the night prayer. Most exegetes said: he delayed it until the last part of the night, because supplication at the time of dawn is not veiled from God. When Jacob reached the appointed time, he advanced to prayer at dawn, and when he finished, he raised his hands to God, the Exalted: "O God, forgive me my grief over Joseph and my lack of patience concerning him, and forgive my sons what they did to Joseph." God revealed to him: "I have forgiven you and them all."

Muharib ibn Dithar said: a paternal uncle of mine used to go to the mosque, and he said: "I passed by the house of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and heard him say: 'O God, You called me and I answered, You commanded me and I obeyed; this is the dawn, so forgive me.'" I asked him about that, and he said: "Jacob delayed the seeking of forgiveness for his sons until the dawn, by his saying: ﴿I will ask my Lord to forgive you﴾."

Ikrimah related from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "'I will ask my Lord to forgive you' means: until the coming of the day of Friday" [128]. Wahb said: he would ask forgiveness for them every Friday night for some twenty-odd years. Tawus said: he delayed it until the dawn of Friday night, and that coincided with the night of 'Ashura'.

From Abu Salamah, from 'Ata' al-Khurasani, who said: "Seeking needs from a young man is easier than from the elderly. Do you not see Joseph's saying to his brothers: ﴿No reproach upon you today﴾, and Jacob's saying (upon him peace): ﴿I will ask my Lord to forgive you﴾?"

Abu al-Hasan al-Mulani al-Sha'bi said: "'I will ask my Lord to forgive you': I will ask Joseph; if he pardons you, I will ask my Lord to forgive you." ﴿Indeed He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾.

It is narrated that when the bearer of good news informed Jacob of Joseph's life, Jacob said: "How did you leave Joseph?" He said: "He is king of Egypt." Jacob said: "What do I want with kingship? On what religion did you leave him?" He said: "On the religion of Islam." Jacob said: "Now the blessing is complete."

Al-Thawri said: When Jacob and Joseph (upon them both peace) met, each embraced the other and they both wept. Joseph said: "O father, you wept for me until your sight was lost; did you not know that the Resurrection will gather us?" He said: "Yes, my son, but I feared that your religion would be stolen, and that I would be separated from you."

They said: Joseph had sent with the bearer of good news to Jacob provisions and two hundred riding-camels, and asked Jacob to come to him with all his family and children. Jacob prepared to leave for Egypt. When he drew near Egypt, the king who was above Joseph went out, and Joseph went out with the king among four thousand troops, and the people of Egypt rode with them to meet Jacob. Jacob was walking, leading his mount, with Yahudha. Jacob looked at the horses and people and said to Yahudha: "Is this the Pharaoh of Egypt?" He said: "No, this is your son."

When each drew near the other, Joseph went to begin with the greeting, but was prevented from doing so, since Jacob had more right to it and was more excellent. So Jacob began the greeting and said: "Peace be upon you, O you who removes sorrows." This is the meaning of His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Then when they entered upon Joseph, he took his parents to himself and said: "Enter Egypt, if God wills, in security."﴾

If it is said: how did Joseph say to them, "Enter Egypt, if God wills, in security," after they had entered it, when God informed us that when they entered upon Joseph and he embraced his parents, he said this to them as he met them before entering Egypt, as we have mentioned?

Some said: in the verse there is inversion and reordering, and this exception is from the saying of Jacob when he said: ﴿I will ask my Lord to forgive you﴾, and the meaning is: "I will ask my Lord to forgive you, if God wills, indeed He is the Forgiving, the Merciful. Then when they entered upon Joseph, he took his parents to himself, and said: 'Enter Egypt... in security,' and he raised his parents upon the throne." This is the meaning of the saying of Abu Jarir. Others said: the exception falls on security, not on entering, like His saying: ﴿You shall enter the Sacred Mosque, if God wills, in security﴾ [Sura al-Fath: 27].

And the saying of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) upon entering the graves: "And we, if God wills, will be joining you" [129] [Sahih Muslim: 1/150]. So the exception falls on joining them, not on death. It was also said: "in" here means "when," like His saying: ﴿And leave what remains of usury, if you are believers﴾ [Sura al-Baqarah: 278], and His saying: ﴿You shall be the uppermost, if you are believers﴾ [Sura Al 'Imran: 139], and His saying: ﴿If they desire chastity﴾ [Sura al-Nur: 33].

Ibn 'Abbas said: He only said "in security" because in the past they had feared the kings of Egypt, and did not enter Egypt, for they had no permit. As for His saying "he took his parents to himself": Ibn Ishaq said: his father and his mother. Others said: his father and his maternal aunt, for Rachel, Joseph's mother, had died in childbirth, and Jacob afterward married her sister Liyya; so he called the aunt "mother," just as he called the paternal uncle "father" in His saying: ﴿We worship your God and the God of your fathers, Abraham and Ishmael and Isaac﴾.

Ishaq related from Bishr, from Sa'id, from al-Hasan, who said: God raised Rachel, Joseph's mother, from her grave until she prostrated, to fulfill the dream.

﴿And he raised his parents upon the throne﴾, on the couch; that is, he seated them upon it. Ibn Ishaq said: it means he raised their status. ﴿And they fell before him in prostration﴾: that is, Jacob, his aunt, and his brothers. At that time the greeting of people was prostration, and by prostration was not meant placing the forehead upon the ground, because that is not permitted except to God, Exalted; it is only bowing and humility as a form of greeting, honor, and salutation, except when it is done in the manner of worship and prayer. This is the saying of al-A'sha ibn Tha'labah:
"When he came to us after the sleep's absence, we prostrated to him and raised the turbans."
Another said:
"Its surplus reins prostrated, as Christians prostrate to their lords."
It was also said: prostration in language means submission, like the saying of al-Nabighah [in the source: Zayd al-Khayl instead of al-Nabighah]:
"With a host in whose lodges the spotted horses are lost; the hills in it are seen prostrating to the hooves."
That is, lowered and humbled.

[Tha'lab] said: "they fell" means "they passed by," and was not meant as falling down and dropping to the ground. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿They did not fall upon them deaf and blind﴾ [Sura al-Furqan: 73]; it only means they did not pass by in that manner. Mujahid: in the sense of passing. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that its meaning is: they fell down to God in prostration, so the "him" refers to God, Exalted.

Joseph then said, and his skin shivered: ﴿This is the interpretation of my vision from before; my Lord has made it true﴾, and that is His saying: ﴿Indeed I saw eleven stars﴾.

They differed about the length of Joseph's absence from Jacob. Al-Kalbi said: two hundred and twenty years. Salman al-Farisi: forty years. Abdullah ibn Shaddad: seventy years. It was also said: seventy-seven years. Al-Hasan said:
Joseph was thrown into the well at seventeen years of age, and was absent from his father eighty years, and lived after his reunion with Jacob twenty-three years, and died at the age of a hundred and twenty years. In the Torah: a hundred and sixteen years. According to Ibn Ishaq ibn Yasar: eighty-seven years. Ibn Abi Ishaq said: eighteen years. Joseph had from the wife of the Aziz: Ephraim, Menasseh, and Rahmah, wife of Job. Between Joseph and Moses were four hundred years.

﴿And He was good to me when He brought me out of the prison﴾; he did not say "out of the well," using courtesy, so as not to remind his brothers of their deed. It was also said: because God's blessing upon him in being saved from prison was greater than His blessing upon him in rescuing him from the well, for his falling into the well was due to his brothers' envy, while his imprisonment was a recompense from God for a slip that had come from him.

﴿And He brought you from the desert﴾, because Jacob and his sons were people of the desert and livestock. "Badw" is the verbal noun of your saying "badā, yabdū, badwan," when one becomes in the desert. ﴿After Satan had stirred discord between me and my brothers﴾. ﴿Indeed my Lord is Gentle, bestowing kindness on whom He wills﴾, knowing the subtleties of matters and their realities. ﴿Indeed He is the Knowing, the Wise﴾.

Abd al-Samad related from his father, from Wahb, who said: They—that is, Jacob and his sons—entered Egypt as seventy-two persons, men and women, and they left with Moses, and their number was six hundred and fifty-some thousand men, besides the offspring, the elderly, and the disabled; and the offspring were a million and two hundred thousand, besides the fighters.

The historians said: Jacob remained in Egypt after his family joined him for twenty-four years in the most pleasant condition and happiest life; then he died in Egypt. When death came to him, he bequeathed to his son Joseph that his body be carried until it was buried beside his father Isaac. Joseph did so, carried it, and buried him in Syria, then returned to Egypt.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: he was transported in a chest of teak to Jerusalem, and that coincided with the day Esau died, and they were buried in one grave. Hence the Jews transport their dead to Jerusalem, those of them who do so. Jacob and Esau were born in one womb and buried in one grave, and their age together was a hundred and forty-seven years.

They said: When God gathered Joseph's family, fulfilled his vision, and cooled his eye, and had made his worldly kingdom and bliss expansive, he knew that this would not last for him and that he must part from it. He desired a bliss more enduring, and his soul longed for Paradise, so he wished for death and supplicated his Lord. No prophet before or after him wished for death, and he said: ﴿My Lord, You have given me of the kingdom﴾, meaning the kingdom of Egypt, ﴿and taught me of the interpretation of events﴾, meaning the interpretation of dreams. ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾, that is, their Creator and Maker.

﴿You are my Guardian in this world and the Hereafter﴾, my helper in this world and the Hereafter, managing my affairs. ﴿Cause me to die a Muslim, and join me with the righteous﴾, with my forefathers the prophets.

It was said: God took him in a good and pure state in Egypt, and he was buried in the Nile in a marble chest. When he died, people quarreled over him, each wanting to be buried in their own quarter, hoping for his blessing, until they gathered to fight. So they decided to bury him in the Nile at the place where the water divides in Egypt, so the water would flow over him and then reach all of Egypt, and they would all share in it equally. They did so.

Salih al-Murri related from Yazid al-Raqashi, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: When God, Mighty and Majestic, gathered Jacob's family, his sons withdrew in private conversation. Some said to others: "Do you not know what you did, and what the old man suffered from you, and what Joseph suffered from you?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Then if they pardon you, but how will you face your Lord?" Their affair settled on coming to the old man, and they sat before him, with Joseph sitting beside his father.

They said: "O our father, we have come to you about a matter we have never come to you about before, and a calamity has befallen us the like of which has never befallen us," until they stirred him, and the prophets (upon them peace) are the most merciful of creatures. He said: "What is wrong with you, my sons?" They said: "Do you not know what we did to you, and what we did to our brother Joseph?" The two said: "Yes." They said: "Have you not both pardoned?" The two said: "Yes." They said: "Then your pardon will not avail us if God has not pardoned us." He said: "Then what do you want, my sons?" They said:

The sons said: "We want you to pray to God. When the revelation comes from God that He has pardoned them, we will have done it; our eyes will be comforted and our hearts will be at rest. Otherwise, there will never be any comfort for our eyes in this world." So the old man (al-Shaykh) faced the qibla and stood, and Yusuf stood behind his father, and they stood behind the two of them, humbled and submissive. Yaʿqub prayed, and Yusuf said "Amin," but He did not answer them for twenty years.

Salih al-Murri said: He kept them in fear. Then, when the twentieth year came, Jibril descended upon Yaʿqub and said:

"Indeed God, blessed and exalted, sent me to you to give you good news: He has answered your supplication concerning your sons, and He has pardoned what they did. For He has taken their covenants after you concerning prophethood. And that is what you mentioned and what you related to me."

When the caravan departed (that is, went out from the outskirts of Egypt heading toward Canaan), their father said: "Indeed, I sense the scent of Joseph" (it is narrated that the wind asked its Lord for permission to bring Jacob the scent of Joseph before the bearer of good news came to him; permission was granted, and it brought it to him). Ibn al-Suddi related from his father, from Mujahid, who said: Jacob caught the scent of Joseph from a distance of three days, because when the wind blew it stirred the shirt and carried the scent of the shirt to Jacob; he found the scent of Paradise, and knew that there is no scent of Paradise on earth except that it comes from that shirt. Therefore he said: "Indeed I sense the scent of Joseph," and he was eight nights' journey away from him.

Shu'bah related from Abu Sinan, who said: I heard Abdullah ibn Abi al-Hudhayl say: I heard Ibn 'Abbas say: Jacob found the scent of Joseph while he was eight nights' journey away from him. Abu Sinan related from Abu Hudhayl, who said: I heard Ibn 'Abbas say: Jacob found the scent of Joseph, and he was eight nights' journey away from him. Shu'bah related from Abu Sinan, who said: I heard Abdullah ibn Abi al-Hudhayl, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning this verse, say: He found its scent from a distance equal to that between Basra and Kufa. Al-Hasan said: It was mentioned to us that between them at that time there were eighty farsakhs.

﴿Unless you think me senile﴾ — Sufyan related from Husayf, from Mujahid, concerning "Unless you think me senile" (la wa-la an tufannidun), he said: "you consider the opinion foolish." From Ibn 'Abbas: "you consider me ignorant." Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Abi Najih related from Mujahid: "lest you say, 'your mind has gone.'" Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Suddi and al-Dahhak said: "you deem me a liar," which is the narration of al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: "you think me senile," and similarly Israil related from Abu Yahya from Mujahid. Al-Rabi' said: "you consider me a fool." Juwaybir related from al-Dahhak: "you think me senile, so you say: 'an old man who has become senile and lost his mind.'" Ibn Yasar said: "you deem me weak." Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: "you find me repugnant." Al-Kisa'i said: "you deem me incapable." Al-Akhfash said: "you blame me." Abu 'Ubaydah said: "you deem me astray."

The root of tafnid (fannada) is corruption. Al-Nabighah said:
"Except Solomon, when the King said to him: 'Stand in the land and restrain it from tafnid.'"
That is, prevent it from corruption. Hence it is said that blame is tafnid. A poet said:
"O my two companions, leave off my blame and my tafnid; what has passed of a matter cannot be returned."
Jarir ibn 'Atiyyah said:
"O my blamers, leave off reproach and be brief; love has lasted long, and you have prolonged tafnid."
Another said:
"You destroyed me with blame and tafnid."
Al-fand is error in speech and opinion. It is said: afnada fulanan al-dahr, meaning when time corrupted him. From the words of Ibn Muqbil:
"Leave time to do what it wills, for when it charges the people with corruption, it corrupts them."

They said — that is, his grandchildren: ﴿By God, you are surely in your old error﴾, your ancient mistake of loving Joseph and not forgetting him.

﴿Then when the bearer of good news came﴾, the one who brought the message of Joseph. Ibn 'Abbas said: the messenger was Yahudha ibn Ya'qub. Ibn Mas'ud said: "the bearer of good news came from ahead of the caravan." Al-Suddi said: Yahudha said: "I was the one who took the shirt stained with blood to Jacob and told him that Joseph had been eaten by the wolf; today I will take the shirt and tell him he is alive, and gladden him as I saddened him." Ibn 'Abbas said: Yahudha carried it alone, apart from them; he went out bareheaded and barefoot and began to run until he reached his father. He had seven loaves with him, which he had not finished eating, and the distance was eighty farsakhs. Al-Dahhak related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: the bearer of good news was Malik ibn Dhu'r from the people of Madyan.

﴿He cast it﴾, that is, the bearer of good news cast Joseph's shirt over Jacob's face, ﴿and he regained his sight﴾: he returned seeing after having been blind.

'Abdullah ibn Ahmad ibn Hanbal related from Abu 'Abdullah al-Sulami, who said: I heard Yahya ibn Muslim, from someone he named, say: Jacob was the most honored of the people of the earth before the Angel of Death, and the Angel of Death asked his Lord for permission to come to Jacob, and was permitted. He came to him, and Jacob said: "O Angel of Death, I ask you by the One who created you: have you taken the soul of Joseph among those you have seized?" He said: "No." The Angel of Death said: "O Jacob, shall I teach you a supplication?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Say: O Possessor of the kindness that never ends and which no one but You can count." So Jacob supplicated with it that night, and the dawn had not risen before he cast the shirt over his face, and he regained his sight. Al-Dahhak said: his sight returned to him after blindness, strength after weakness, youth after decrepitude, and joy after sorrow.

He said: ﴿Did I not tell you that I know from God what you do not know﴾, concerning Joseph's life and that God would reunite us. They said, after that: ﴿O our father, ask forgiveness for us for our sins; indeed we have been sinners﴾, those who were at fault.

Jacob (upon him peace) said: ﴿I will ask my Lord to forgive you﴾ in the night prayer. Most exegetes said: he delayed it until the last part of the night, because supplication at the time of dawn is not veiled from God. When Jacob reached the appointed time, he advanced to prayer at dawn, and when he finished, he raised his hands to God, the Exalted: "O God, forgive me my grief over Joseph and my lack of patience concerning him, and forgive my sons what they did to Joseph." God revealed to him: "I have forgiven you and them all."

Muharib ibn Dithar said: a paternal uncle of mine used to go to the mosque, and he said: "I passed by the house of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and heard him say: 'O God, You called me and I answered, You commanded me and I obeyed; this is the dawn, so forgive me.'" I asked him about that, and he said: "Jacob delayed the seeking of forgiveness for his sons until the dawn, by his saying: ﴿I will ask my Lord to forgive you﴾."

Ikrimah related from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "'I will ask my Lord to forgive you' means: until the coming of the day of Friday" [128]. Wahb said: he would ask forgiveness for them every Friday night for some twenty-odd years. Tawus said: he delayed it until the dawn of Friday night, and that coincided with the night of 'Ashura'.

From Abu Salamah, from 'Ata' al-Khurasani, who said: "Seeking needs from a young man is easier than from the elderly. Do you not see Joseph's saying to his brothers: ﴿No reproach upon you today﴾, and Jacob's saying (upon him peace): ﴿I will ask my Lord to forgive you﴾?"

Abu al-Hasan al-Mulani al-Sha'bi said: "'I will ask my Lord to forgive you': I will ask Joseph; if he pardons you, I will ask my Lord to forgive you." ﴿Indeed He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾.

It is narrated that when the bearer of good news informed Jacob of Joseph's life, Jacob said: "How did you leave Joseph?" He said: "He is king of Egypt." Jacob said: "What do I want with kingship? On what religion did you leave him?" He said: "On the religion of Islam." Jacob said: "Now the blessing is complete."

Al-Thawri said: When Jacob and Joseph (upon them both peace) met, each embraced the other and they both wept. Joseph said: "O father, you wept for me until your sight was lost; did you not know that the Resurrection will gather us?" He said: "Yes, my son, but I feared that your religion would be stolen, and that I would be separated from you."

They said: Joseph had sent with the bearer of good news to Jacob provisions and two hundred riding-camels, and asked Jacob to come to him with all his family and children. Jacob prepared to leave for Egypt. When he drew near Egypt, the king who was above Joseph went out, and Joseph went out with the king among four thousand troops, and the people of Egypt rode with them to meet Jacob. Jacob was walking, leading his mount, with Yahudha. Jacob looked at the horses and people and said to Yahudha: "Is this the Pharaoh of Egypt?" He said: "No, this is your son."

When each drew near the other, Joseph went to begin with the greeting, but was prevented from doing so, since Jacob had more right to it and was more excellent. So Jacob began the greeting and said: "Peace be upon you, O you who removes sorrows." This is the meaning of His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Then when they entered upon Joseph, he took his parents to himself and said: "Enter Egypt, if God wills, in security."﴾

If it is said: how did Joseph say to them, "Enter Egypt, if God wills, in security," after they had entered it, when God informed us that when they entered upon Joseph and he embraced his parents, he said this to them as he met them before entering Egypt, as we have mentioned?

Some said: in the verse there is inversion and reordering, and this exception is from the saying of Jacob when he said: ﴿I will ask my Lord to forgive you﴾, and the meaning is: "I will ask my Lord to forgive you, if God wills, indeed He is the Forgiving, the Merciful. Then when they entered upon Joseph, he took his parents to himself, and said: 'Enter Egypt... in security,' and he raised his parents upon the throne." This is the meaning of the saying of Abu Jarir. Others said: the exception falls on security, not on entering, like His saying: ﴿You shall enter the Sacred Mosque, if God wills, in security﴾ [Sura al-Fath: 27].

And the saying of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) upon entering the graves: "And we, if God wills, will be joining you" [129] [Sahih Muslim: 1/150]. So the exception falls on joining them, not on death. It was also said: "in" here means "when," like His saying: ﴿And leave what remains of usury, if you are believers﴾ [Sura al-Baqarah: 278], and His saying: ﴿You shall be the uppermost, if you are believers﴾ [Sura Al 'Imran: 139], and His saying: ﴿If they desire chastity﴾ [Sura al-Nur: 33].

Ibn 'Abbas said: He only said "in security" because in the past they had feared the kings of Egypt, and did not enter Egypt, for they had no permit. As for His saying "he took his parents to himself": Ibn Ishaq said: his father and his mother. Others said: his father and his maternal aunt, for Rachel, Joseph's mother, had died in childbirth, and Jacob afterward married her sister Liyya; so he called the aunt "mother," just as he called the paternal uncle "father" in His saying: ﴿We worship your God and the God of your fathers, Abraham and Ishmael and Isaac﴾.

Ishaq related from Bishr, from Sa'id, from al-Hasan, who said: God raised Rachel, Joseph's mother, from her grave until she prostrated, to fulfill the dream.

﴿And he raised his parents upon the throne﴾, on the couch; that is, he seated them upon it. Ibn Ishaq said: it means he raised their status. ﴿And they fell before him in prostration﴾: that is, Jacob, his aunt, and his brothers. At that time the greeting of people was prostration, and by prostration was not meant placing the forehead upon the ground, because that is not permitted except to God, Exalted; it is only bowing and humility as a form of greeting, honor, and salutation, except when it is done in the manner of worship and prayer. This is the saying of al-A'sha ibn Tha'labah:
"When he came to us after the sleep's absence, we prostrated to him and raised the turbans."
Another said:
"Its surplus reins prostrated, as Christians prostrate to their lords."
It was also said: prostration in language means submission, like the saying of al-Nabighah [in the source: Zayd al-Khayl instead of al-Nabighah]:
"With a host in whose lodges the spotted horses are lost; the hills in it are seen prostrating to the hooves."
That is, lowered and humbled.

[Tha'lab] said: "they fell" means "they passed by," and was not meant as falling down and dropping to the ground. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿They did not fall upon them deaf and blind﴾ [Sura al-Furqan: 73]; it only means they did not pass by in that manner. Mujahid: in the sense of passing. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that its meaning is: they fell down to God in prostration, so the "him" refers to God, Exalted.

Joseph then said, and his skin shivered: ﴿This is the interpretation of my vision from before; my Lord has made it true﴾, and that is His saying: ﴿Indeed I saw eleven stars﴾.

They differed about the length of Joseph's absence from Jacob. Al-Kalbi said: two hundred and twenty years. Salman al-Farisi: forty years. Abdullah ibn Shaddad: seventy years. It was also said: seventy-seven years. Al-Hasan said:
Joseph was thrown into the well at seventeen years of age, and was absent from his father eighty years, and lived after his reunion with Jacob twenty-three years, and died at the age of a hundred and twenty years. In the Torah: a hundred and sixteen years. According to Ibn Ishaq ibn Yasar: eighty-seven years. Ibn Abi Ishaq said: eighteen years. Joseph had from the wife of the Aziz: Ephraim, Menasseh, and Rahmah, wife of Job. Between Joseph and Moses were four hundred years.

﴿And He was good to me when He brought me out of the prison﴾; he did not say "out of the well," using courtesy, so as not to remind his brothers of their deed. It was also said: because God's blessing upon him in being saved from prison was greater than His blessing upon him in rescuing him from the well, for his falling into the well was due to his brothers' envy, while his imprisonment was a recompense from God for a slip that had come from him.

﴿And He brought you from the desert﴾, because Jacob and his sons were people of the desert and livestock. "Badw" is the verbal noun of your saying "badā, yabdū, badwan," when one becomes in the desert. ﴿After Satan had stirred discord between me and my brothers﴾. ﴿Indeed my Lord is Gentle, bestowing kindness on whom He wills﴾, knowing the subtleties of matters and their realities. ﴿Indeed He is the Knowing, the Wise﴾.

Abd al-Samad related from his father, from Wahb, who said: They—that is, Jacob and his sons—entered Egypt as seventy-two persons, men and women, and they left with Moses, and their number was six hundred and fifty-some thousand men, besides the offspring, the elderly, and the disabled; and the offspring were a million and two hundred thousand, besides the fighters.

The historians said: Jacob remained in Egypt after his family joined him for twenty-four years in the most pleasant condition and happiest life; then he died in Egypt. When death came to him, he bequeathed to his son Joseph that his body be carried until it was buried beside his father Isaac. Joseph did so, carried it, and buried him in Syria, then returned to Egypt.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: he was transported in a chest of teak to Jerusalem, and that coincided with the day Esau died, and they were buried in one grave. Hence the Jews transport their dead to Jerusalem, those of them who do so. Jacob and Esau were born in one womb and buried in one grave, and their age together was a hundred and forty-seven years.

They said: When God gathered Joseph's family, fulfilled his vision, and cooled his eye, and had made his worldly kingdom and bliss expansive, he knew that this would not last for him and that he must part from it. He desired a bliss more enduring, and his soul longed for Paradise, so he wished for death and supplicated his Lord. No prophet before or after him wished for death, and he said: ﴿My Lord, You have given me of the kingdom﴾, meaning the kingdom of Egypt, ﴿and taught me of the interpretation of events﴾, meaning the interpretation of dreams. ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾, that is, their Creator and Maker.

﴿You are my Guardian in this world and the Hereafter﴾, my helper in this world and the Hereafter, managing my affairs. ﴿Cause me to die a Muslim, and join me with the righteous﴾, with my forefathers the prophets.

It was said: God took him in a good and pure state in Egypt, and he was buried in the Nile in a marble chest. When he died, people quarreled over him, each wanting to be buried in their own quarter, hoping for his blessing, until they gathered to fight. So they decided to bury him in the Nile at the place where the water divides in Egypt, so the water would flow over him and then reach all of Egypt, and they would all share in it equally. They did so.

Salih al-Murri related from Yazid al-Raqashi, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: When God, Mighty and Majestic, gathered Jacob's family, his sons withdrew in private conversation. Some said to others: "Do you not know what you did, and what the old man suffered from you, and what Joseph suffered from you?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Then if they pardon you, but how will you face your Lord?" Their affair settled on coming to the old man, and they sat before him, with Joseph sitting beside his father.

They said: "O our father, we have come to you about a matter we have never come to you about before, and a calamity has befallen us the like of which has never befallen us," until they stirred him, and the prophets (upon them peace) are the most merciful of creatures. He said: "What is wrong with you, my sons?" They said: "Do you not know what we did to you, and what we did to our brother Joseph?" The two said: "Yes." They said: "Have you not both pardoned?" The two said: "Yes." They said: "Then your pardon will not avail us if God has not pardoned us." He said: "Then what do you want, my sons?" They said:

The sons said: "We want you to pray to God. When the revelation comes from God that He has pardoned them, we will have done it; our eyes will be comforted and our hearts will be at rest. Otherwise, there will never be any comfort for our eyes in this world." So the old man (al-Shaykh) faced the qibla and stood, and Yusuf stood behind his father, and they stood behind the two of them, humbled and submissive. Yaʿqub prayed, and Yusuf said "Amin," but He did not answer them for twenty years.

Salih al-Murri said: He kept them in fear. Then, when the twentieth year came, Jibril descended upon Yaʿqub and said:

"Indeed God, blessed and exalted, sent me to you to give you good news: He has answered your supplication concerning your sons, and He has pardoned what they did. For He has taken their covenants after you concerning prophethood. And that is what you mentioned and what you related to me."

When the caravan departed (that is, went out from the outskirts of Egypt heading toward Canaan), their father said: "Indeed, I sense the scent of Joseph" (it is narrated that the wind asked its Lord for permission to bring Jacob the scent of Joseph before the bearer of good news came to him; permission was granted, and it brought it to him). Ibn al-Suddi related from his father, from Mujahid, who said: Jacob caught the scent of Joseph from a distance of three days, because when the wind blew it stirred the shirt and carried the scent of the shirt to Jacob; he found the scent of Paradise, and knew that there is no scent of Paradise on earth except that it comes from that shirt. Therefore he said: "Indeed I sense the scent of Joseph," and he was eight nights' journey away from him.

Shu'bah related from Abu Sinan, who said: I heard Abdullah ibn Abi al-Hudhayl say: I heard Ibn 'Abbas say: Jacob found the scent of Joseph while he was eight nights' journey away from him. Abu Sinan related from Abu Hudhayl, who said: I heard Ibn 'Abbas say: Jacob found the scent of Joseph, and he was eight nights' journey away from him. Shu'bah related from Abu Sinan, who said: I heard Abdullah ibn Abi al-Hudhayl, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning this verse, say: He found its scent from a distance equal to that between Basra and Kufa. Al-Hasan said: It was mentioned to us that between them at that time there were eighty farsakhs.

﴿Unless you think me senile﴾ — Sufyan related from Husayf, from Mujahid, concerning "Unless you think me senile" (la wa-la an tufannidun), he said: "you consider the opinion foolish." From Ibn 'Abbas: "you consider me ignorant." Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Abi Najih related from Mujahid: "lest you say, 'your mind has gone.'" Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Suddi and al-Dahhak said: "you deem me a liar," which is the narration of al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: "you think me senile," and similarly Israil related from Abu Yahya from Mujahid. Al-Rabi' said: "you consider me a fool." Juwaybir related from al-Dahhak: "you think me senile, so you say: 'an old man who has become senile and lost his mind.'" Ibn Yasar said: "you deem me weak." Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: "you find me repugnant." Al-Kisa'i said: "you deem me incapable." Al-Akhfash said: "you blame me." Abu 'Ubaydah said: "you deem me astray."

The root of tafnid (fannada) is corruption. Al-Nabighah said:
"Except Solomon, when the King said to him: 'Stand in the land and restrain it from tafnid.'"
That is, prevent it from corruption. Hence it is said that blame is tafnid. A poet said:
"O my two companions, leave off my blame and my tafnid; what has passed of a matter cannot be returned."
Jarir ibn 'Atiyyah said:
"O my blamers, leave off reproach and be brief; love has lasted long, and you have prolonged tafnid."
Another said:
"You destroyed me with blame and tafnid."
Al-fand is error in speech and opinion. It is said: afnada fulanan al-dahr, meaning when time corrupted him. From the words of Ibn Muqbil:
"Leave time to do what it wills, for when it charges the people with corruption, it corrupts them."

They said — that is, his grandchildren: ﴿By God, you are surely in your old error﴾, your ancient mistake of loving Joseph and not forgetting him.

﴿Then when the bearer of good news came﴾, the one who brought the message of Joseph. Ibn 'Abbas said: the messenger was Yahudha ibn Ya'qub. Ibn Mas'ud said: "the bearer of good news came from ahead of the caravan." Al-Suddi said: Yahudha said: "I was the one who took the shirt stained with blood to Jacob and told him that Joseph had been eaten by the wolf; today I will take the shirt and tell him he is alive, and gladden him as I saddened him." Ibn 'Abbas said: Yahudha carried it alone, apart from them; he went out bareheaded and barefoot and began to run until he reached his father. He had seven loaves with him, which he had not finished eating, and the distance was eighty farsakhs. Al-Dahhak related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: the bearer of good news was Malik ibn Dhu'r from the people of Madyan.

﴿He cast it﴾, that is, the bearer of good news cast Joseph's shirt over Jacob's face, ﴿and he regained his sight﴾: he returned seeing after having been blind.

'Abdullah ibn Ahmad ibn Hanbal related from Abu 'Abdullah al-Sulami, who said: I heard Yahya ibn Muslim, from someone he named, say: Jacob was the most honored of the people of the earth before the Angel of Death, and the Angel of Death asked his Lord for permission to come to Jacob, and was permitted. He came to him, and Jacob said: "O Angel of Death, I ask you by the One who created you: have you taken the soul of Joseph among those you have seized?" He said: "No." The Angel of Death said: "O Jacob, shall I teach you a supplication?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Say: O Possessor of the kindness that never ends and which no one but You can count." So Jacob supplicated with it that night, and the dawn had not risen before he cast the shirt over his face, and he regained his sight. Al-Dahhak said: his sight returned to him after blindness, strength after weakness, youth after decrepitude, and joy after sorrow.

He said: ﴿Did I not tell you that I know from God what you do not know﴾, concerning Joseph's life and that God would reunite us. They said, after that: ﴿O our father, ask forgiveness for us for our sins; indeed we have been sinners﴾, those who were at fault.

Jacob (upon him peace) said: ﴿I will ask my Lord to forgive you﴾ in the night prayer. Most exegetes said: he delayed it until the last part of the night, because supplication at the time of dawn is not veiled from God. When Jacob reached the appointed time, he advanced to prayer at dawn, and when he finished, he raised his hands to God, the Exalted: "O God, forgive me my grief over Joseph and my lack of patience concerning him, and forgive my sons what they did to Joseph." God revealed to him: "I have forgiven you and them all."

Muharib ibn Dithar said: a paternal uncle of mine used to go to the mosque, and he said: "I passed by the house of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and heard him say: 'O God, You called me and I answered, You commanded me and I obeyed; this is the dawn, so forgive me.'" I asked him about that, and he said: "Jacob delayed the seeking of forgiveness for his sons until the dawn, by his saying: ﴿I will ask my Lord to forgive you﴾."

Ikrimah related from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "'I will ask my Lord to forgive you' means: until the coming of the day of Friday" [128]. Wahb said: he would ask forgiveness for them every Friday night for some twenty-odd years. Tawus said: he delayed it until the dawn of Friday night, and that coincided with the night of 'Ashura'.

From Abu Salamah, from 'Ata' al-Khurasani, who said: "Seeking needs from a young man is easier than from the elderly. Do you not see Joseph's saying to his brothers: ﴿No reproach upon you today﴾, and Jacob's saying (upon him peace): ﴿I will ask my Lord to forgive you﴾?"

Abu al-Hasan al-Mulani al-Sha'bi said: "'I will ask my Lord to forgive you': I will ask Joseph; if he pardons you, I will ask my Lord to forgive you." ﴿Indeed He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾.

It is narrated that when the bearer of good news informed Jacob of Joseph's life, Jacob said: "How did you leave Joseph?" He said: "He is king of Egypt." Jacob said: "What do I want with kingship? On what religion did you leave him?" He said: "On the religion of Islam." Jacob said: "Now the blessing is complete."

Al-Thawri said: When Jacob and Joseph (upon them both peace) met, each embraced the other and they both wept. Joseph said: "O father, you wept for me until your sight was lost; did you not know that the Resurrection will gather us?" He said: "Yes, my son, but I feared that your religion would be stolen, and that I would be separated from you."

They said: Joseph had sent with the bearer of good news to Jacob provisions and two hundred riding-camels, and asked Jacob to come to him with all his family and children. Jacob prepared to leave for Egypt. When he drew near Egypt, the king who was above Joseph went out, and Joseph went out with the king among four thousand troops, and the people of Egypt rode with them to meet Jacob. Jacob was walking, leading his mount, with Yahudha. Jacob looked at the horses and people and said to Yahudha: "Is this the Pharaoh of Egypt?" He said: "No, this is your son."

When each drew near the other, Joseph went to begin with the greeting, but was prevented from doing so, since Jacob had more right to it and was more excellent. So Jacob began the greeting and said: "Peace be upon you, O you who removes sorrows." This is the meaning of His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Then when they entered upon Joseph, he took his parents to himself and said: "Enter Egypt, if God wills, in security."﴾

If it is said: how did Joseph say to them, "Enter Egypt, if God wills, in security," after they had entered it, when God informed us that when they entered upon Joseph and he embraced his parents, he said this to them as he met them before entering Egypt, as we have mentioned?

Some said: in the verse there is inversion and reordering, and this exception is from the saying of Jacob when he said: ﴿I will ask my Lord to forgive you﴾, and the meaning is: "I will ask my Lord to forgive you, if God wills, indeed He is the Forgiving, the Merciful. Then when they entered upon Joseph, he took his parents to himself, and said: 'Enter Egypt... in security,' and he raised his parents upon the throne." This is the meaning of the saying of Abu Jarir. Others said: the exception falls on security, not on entering, like His saying: ﴿You shall enter the Sacred Mosque, if God wills, in security﴾ [Sura al-Fath: 27].

And the saying of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) upon entering the graves: "And we, if God wills, will be joining you" [129] [Sahih Muslim: 1/150]. So the exception falls on joining them, not on death.
